utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We trust you're all refreshed from the break. Mr. Cayley, you have a motion, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. May it please Your Honours. It's simply -- it's actually two matters. They are linked. The first is the motion of the 7th of January in respect of the protective measures for the next witness, which I think is self-explanatory. I don't understand there are any objections from the Defence, but you might wish to hear them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection that anybody wishes to make? If not, I don't encourage you to rise. The Chamber is of the view, Mr. Cayley, that your motion as spelled out in paragraph 6 of the written motion should be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, one further matter linked to this particular application is that there are a number of documents that the witness will be putting into evidence, and I will distribute the binder containing those documents. They -- the majority of them, apart from about five documents which I can identify as we go along, need to be under seal because they were originally provided to us under Rule 70 the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but I can make that application at the end of this witness's evidence. And finally linked to that, behind me are two representatives of the British government who are here in connection with this evidence. On the left is Mr. Dominic Raab, who is the legal advisor to the British embassy, and on the right is Katharine Shepherd, who is a legal advisor with the Ministry of Defence. And they are here, Your Honour, as special advisors to the Prosecutor on the issue of Rule 70 and these documents. So any intervention that they may wish to make in respect of compliance with the Rule 70 regime they would make through me and by speaking to me in a break. So I would merely, Your Honour, ask your permission that they be present in the courtroom during the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There would be no difficulty, as they are present in the capacity of advisors to the Prosecution in respect of the witness, not in any independent role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that is understood and accepted. Are we ready to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are. If the witness could be brought in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the order, the shutters will need to be shut for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting I'm wondering if Your Honours have in front of you a tabbed binder with 42 -- yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 42, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you would be kind enough to take the affirmation which is on the card which offered to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would please be seated. Now, should we be in private or public session for these opening questions, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I've designed the examination-in-chief such that we don't need to be in private session. I'm not going to refer to the sensitive matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The shutters can go up then. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sir, just to remind you. I know you testified previously in the Milosevic case, but if you can pause between my question and your answer because there are interpreters between us. And I will try and set a fairly slow and steady pace so that we don't run ahead of the interpreters. Now, am I right in saying that you are a retired British army colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that you were commissioned into the parachute regiment in 1967?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And at what levels of command have you had experience in the establish army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I've commanded up to battalion and above level, to brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how many individuals does that involve?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's upwards of 1.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you have any combat experience? Have you had combat experience during your career?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I've had probably rather too much combat experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just say briefly, give one example with where you've had experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I've had four years in the Middle East commanding up to 3.000 men in a fairly major war. I've been in the Falklands, I've been in Northern Ireland, and I've been in the Balkans and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm right in saying that in 1996 you were appointed as the defence attache to the British embassy in Belgrade, in Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Or Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges the role of the defence attache within an embassy, and specifically within the British embassy in Belgrade at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As the defence attache for your country, you are accredited directly as your chief of defence staff's representative in the country which is Yugoslavia. You have direct access to the chief of defence staff and other senior officers within in the Vojska Jugoslavije, the Yugoslav army, and it is your job to represent any military problems to these people at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just intervene, Mr. Cayley, to indicate it may be necessary to slow the rate of evidence. We have to go through more than one stage of translation, as you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm actually trying to listen to the French and as it finishes, I'll ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in your role as defence attache, you would also advise the ambassador, himself or herself, on military matters within the country. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. The -- usually the ambassador would use a diplomatic telegram, or a DipTel for short, in which I would add the security paragraph as I thought fit, bearing on the events that the ambassador was reporting, which would be on a daily or more than frequent basis if that is what is required. And these were different, sorry, to the military telegrams that I would send as and when required back to the Ministry of Defence in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And where -- and the DipTel that you've just referred to, where was that sent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That would go back to the foreign office, from the foreign commonwealth's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness can be provided with the binder, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond and we can show an example of one of these DipTels. Could we place one on the screen if it's in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, if you could take the map and place that on the ELMO next to you. Now, this is a map that I think you've provided to us which you used at the time of your service in Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could turn to the first tab in that binder, which I think is a diplomatic telegram dated the 2nd of March of 1998. Is that -- is that a DipTel, just so that we all understand what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, and it is signed by the current -- the then-current ambassador or his deputy head of mission or even the first political officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And who gave input into these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Primarily this is the vehicle that the -- our ambassador would use or his deputy head of mission, or the first officer political, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you provided input on security matters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, specifically in respect of your role in Serbia -- in Yugoslavia, rather, as it then was, did you have occasion to visit Kosovo during your time in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I spent from about 90 -- the early part of 1998 up until 1999 when NATO bombed Yugoslavia. I spent more or less most of my time touring the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because that was my task to ascertain what was going on in this province of Serbia, Yugoslavia, and because I hadn't -- HMD government to know -- [French on the English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there's a problem, Your Honour, with the translation. It says there's French on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suggest you might press on. It may be self-sorting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can get you to direct your mind to February of -- in fact, March of 1998 and the first diplomatic telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said, it is my intention to actually read these into the record. I know it will take time, but it does ensure that there is a public record of the content of these documents which are going to be under seal. So it will actually make the evidence available to the public. Some of the sections that I'm going to read are longer than others, some are quite short, some are quite long. I'll see for how we go with time in respect of doing that with each and every one. But that is what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It -- let me read the first one, Mr. Crosland, and then I will ask you a number of questions. This is a diplomatic telegram dated the 2nd of March, 1998, subject: Kosovo, major incident in Drenica. "Major conflict between police and Albanians in Drenica area over the weekend. Even government press acknowledge 16 Albanians (terrorists) and four policemen dead. Albanian claim dead include at least one woman and a 16-year-old boy. Final casualty figures may be higher. Still unclear who made the first move. Police claim to have uncovered sizeable arms caches. Fighting seems to have ceased for now." There's then reference to a demonstration in Pristina, which I won't read out in paragraph 2. Paragraph 3: "Most of the fighting took place near Glogovac, about 40 kilometres west of Pristina. The official line is that terrorists attacked a police patrol, inflicting casualties, and that the police responded and conducted a manhunt for the attackers. The official media copied by others report that police uncovered substantial caches of weapons and explosives. Comment may be true. The Albanian side claim that the incidents started with the police chasing a car into the Drenica area as part of their clamp-down on suspect activity. The fighting seems to have started around midday on 28 February and continued until late on 1 March. There are no confirmed reports of further fighting so far. "The final casualties may never become entirely clear. The government press are saying four policemen and 16 Albanians described as terrorists were killed. But there is good reason to suspect that the final figures may be somewhat higher. On the police side, it appears that men from the special anti-terrorist forces were deployed, and two of these may have been killed. The picture on the Albanian side is even less clear with telephone lines to the Drenica area still cut off. Some of the wounded Albanians have apparently refused to go to state hospitals. More reliable Albanian reports claim that at least one woman and one 16-year-old boy were among those killed. Milosevic, Milutinovic, and Minic have all sent messages of sympathy to the families of the dead police officers. Milosevic's tone was uncompromising." Now, Mr. Crosland, were you aware of that event taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This incident took place on the date stated, and I and another defence attache arrived down and were the first people to make an overview of the entire area. And we were given very good access by the Yugoslav authorities, for whatever reason, I don't know. And this really refers to the incident where the two families, the Jashari and Ahmeti families, were attacked by the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the Serbian security forces attack these two families, the Ahmeti and Jashari families, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These two families had, how would you put it, form in the various deals that were done in the province of Kosovo, and there was indications that they were involved within the then-fledgling Kosovo Liberation Army movement, or UCK, which was a growing problem, or beginning to be a growing problem within the province Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you said they had form, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They were probably a part of the Albanian Mafia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you given any indications by the Serbs of what activities these families were involved in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. As I said, they -- the claim was that they were involved with the fledgling K -- Kosovo Liberation Army at that particular point in time. And if may point out to Your Honours, the Drenica area is this area just to the west of Pristina and was the initial place where the Kosovo Liberation Army started to carry out operations as has just been described by Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you know, do know why the attack started on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The attack started because four policemen were killed at a place called Rudnik, which is up on the northern route, across to Pec over here, and it was a follow-up on that particular attack on the Minister of Interior that the Serbs mounted this combined operation of probably about 500 men with armoured vehicles and other forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have a highlighter? Because I would like you to mark these locations. We're not going to number them because I don't that is necessary, but I think it would be a good idea if you marked certainly the area where these policemen were killed at Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know the location of where the actual attack on the Ahmeti and Jashari families took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It took place north of a little village called Srbica and a place called Donji Prekaz, which is in the area where I'm marking now. The area of the Drenica is this valley area bounded by the two roads. If it helps Your Honours for me to go round the map, I don't know how familiar people are with the countryside of Kosovo. We keep referring to towns and things, it may be useful if I point them out to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll as we go along --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Cayley will guide you in that direction. We are gaining a limited familiarity already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As we go through each DipTel, I'll ask you to mark off the particular places that you refer to. How long did the fighting go on between the police and the Jashari and Ahmeti families as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: For about 36 hours on an on-and-off basis roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see subsequently the aftermath of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We drove into the area concerned, and the two major houses involved with this particular fight were extremely badly damaged, having had armoured vehicles within 10 to 15 metres of the house. There were many heavy calibre shells, empty shells on the ground, indicating a very fierce fight, and eventually the bodies were returned sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The bodies of whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Yes. We saw all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Most of these bodies had been shot at very close range, indicating that a very close-range fire fight had taken place, and there were elderly people as well as women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many bodies did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there were 16 and then a further 10 were also produced at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many women and children?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't honestly remember, but there were some women and children amongst the bodies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many elderly people; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It depends what you call elderly, but over fighting age, I would say four or five, if my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What, if any, was the significance of this event?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think the Serbian security forces were intent on attempting to rub out a terrorist movement that had started to come to light in the early '90s. And in about 1996/1997, we certainly knew that there were indications that the Kosovo Liberation Army as a fledgling organisation - and I state very much as a fledgling organisation - was intent on looking at the province of Kosovo as an additional state outside of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can move on to the next telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is at tab 3, Your Honours, it's behind tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this diplomatic telegram is dated the 9th of March, 1998. Subject: Kosovo: Situation report at 0800 hours, 9 March. "Summary. 1. Police action continuing in Lausa region, south-west of Prekaz. Report of one Albanian killed by sniper fire. Visiting diplomats confirm heavy damage in Prekaz, but to a limited number of buildings. Attention now focuses on today's demonstrations." Paragraph 2: "Main road through Drenica area remains open. DA, defence attache, has crossed this morning and reports continuing police operations in the area of Klina/Lausa, south-west of Prekaz. He could not leave the main road. Separately we have heard reports of one Albanian being killed by police snipers in Lausa. Again, consistent with media reports quoting police sources as saying that there remain some terrorists to be dealt with. "The Canadian ambassador, who was in the party of diplomats which visited Prekaz on 8 March, has confirmed great devastation to a limited number of buildings with evidence of attack by heavy weapons and mortars. He also confirms continuing heavy police presence and a complete absence of civilian activity in an area that normally would be bustling." Mr. Crosland, if you could please point out for us on the map and mark them. If you can show Their Honours where the Lausa region and in particular Prekaz is located.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prekaz is just north of Srbica which is not marked. Srbica is here. And then the small hamlet, little village of Lausa is just in this area here. We were working in a very small area and the main road that it refers to runs from Gornji Klina in the north down to what is called the Komorane crossroads in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see these operations taking place on the 9th of March in this area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We visited the area throughout the 9th and the 10th of March. And the Canadian ambassador's remarks and also by an experienced combat officer myself, I would confirm there was heavy -- very heavy usage of heavy weapons with devastating attacks on the two houses, particularly the Ahmeti and Jashari compounds. Other houses had either been torched, burned, or fired at. There was still extremely heavy Serb security force presence, mainly of the Ministry of Interior, the police, and associated special forces within the police element, that involved armoured personnel carriers, and other heavy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this operation that you saw on the 9th of March connected with the operation that you'd seen in respect of the Ahmeti and Jashari family earlier in the month?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had operations, as far as you know, been continuing since the beginning of March through to the 9th of March, or had they been intermittent? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The initial fire fight lasted for, as I said, 36 hours on and off. And then the Serbian security forces as was normal throughout the whole conflict would then try to maintain control of the area by having various security posts, defended posts, all the way along the area, and they would man these with whatever was required in the way of troops and armoured vehicles. So in effect they controlled the area insomuch as -- where they could see. And as I've pointed out on the map, the area of Lausa is only about two kilometres away, and that was in KLA hands. So it gives you some idea of the intricacy of the operations that were to continue throughout the whole of 1998 and into 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So just to clarify, during the course of this operation the village of Lausa was under the control of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And that was literally 500 metres from the nearest Serbian checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on to the next DipTel. This is behind tab 4, and this is dated the 11th of March of 1998. And the only paragraph that I want to refer to is paragraph 11, although I think there is a reference to information that you provided in paragraph 10. But I'm only interested in paragraph 11. "Tanjug reports that there have been a number of grenade attacks on Albanian restaurants and businesses in Pec. According to Tanjug, these were the work of the KLA against businessmen who collaborate with the Serb manifestation." Can you point out where Pec is located?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Pec is the -- one of the major towns in the west of Kosovo and houses the very famous monastery of the Serbian Orthodox church just to the west. It was a bustling town of both Serbian and Albanian ethnic groups. A lot of business came out of this area, including the major factory which contained beer, which is of a critical nature to the Serbs, and these attacks that are alluded to by Tanjug were similar of what went on throughout this campaign, where Albanians who seemed to be siding with the Serb administration were taken out and their businesses either bombed and they themselves murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see yourself any of these damaged businesses, because this is a newspaper report. Did you see them in Pec at all yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We didn't see this particular one, no. But I saw later on many businesses that were wrecked purely for that business -- reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, what reason is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That they had sided -- or according to the Serbs -- sorry, to the KLA, they had sided with the Serbs and therefore retribution was taken against them by members of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next DipTel, which is behind tab 5, and this is dated the 24th of March, 1998. And here we move to a different area of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Kosovo. And I'll read it out. Paragraphs 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Decani. 2: "My DA has confirmed local media reports of exchanges of fire in several villages between Decani and Djakovica (about 60 kilometres south-west of Pristina, not in Drenica). According to the state-controlled radio Pristina, the exchanges began when a terrorist group opened fire on a police patrol this morning. The police returned fire and the Albanians barricaded themselves into local houses. There are various reports of casualties: One policeman and five Albanians killed; one policeman and 10 Albanians injured. There have also been suggestions that some Albanians have been arrested. My DA has reported that at approximately 1130 Zulu, shots were heard in Riznic, 10 kilometres south-east of Decani from a police helicopter. There were two explosions, followed by an exchange of fire lasting 20 minutes. "The Kosovo information centre close to Rugova's LDK have condemned the police action alleging that some villages were surrounded and houses set on fire. The independent Albanian media is reporting that three houses were destroyed. There are also Albanian claims that villagers have fled the area. It appears that the operation is still taking place and that the area has now been sealed off." Let's deal with that first, Mr. Crosland, before actually moving to the next paragraphs. Can you indicate this area on the map, the villages between Decani and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the area is in the western area of Kosovo. Decani, here, another monastery area, and Djakovica on the western side of Kosovo. It's along the main road that goes from Pec to Decani, through Djakovica and down to Prizren that was to become a important line for the Serbian security forces to attempt to hold in later exchanges with the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, do you remember this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you add anything to what is actually in the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not -- nothing in particular. This was just an indication that the conflict, having spread from the area of the Drenica just to the west of Pristina, was now coming over to the western side, which was not -- was nothing unusual to us because it was clear from an early stage that reinforcements and resupplies were coming in over the Albanian border, what I would call the corridor through to Decani and then on into Klina and on into the Drenica to supply men in the eastern area with the equipment to continue the conflict against the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've just said resupplies were coming in -- reinforcements and resupplies were coming in over the Albanian border. For which side? For the Serbs or for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: For the Kosovo Liberation Army. I mean, these, as people are well aware, are traditional smuggling routes from Albania which have been used since the silk route was started from Dubrovnik down Prizren in the south-west here and on to Constantinople. Or Istanbul, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this report also refers to shots being heard in the village of Riznic. Is Riznic marked -- can you mark it on this map? I don't know whether it's --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Riznic is to the east of the major town of Decani. These are all very small hamlets or villages of 20 or 30 houses in a rural setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At this time did you -- the report refers to Rugova complaining about houses being set on fire. Do you recall seeing that at all in any of these villages at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This was to be a sad reflection of the whole conflict throughout 1998 and 1999, and I think later on I mentioned that something like over 200 to 400 villages were purposely and wantonly destroyed by the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on this particular occasion you saw these houses on fire? You saw these houses being fired --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if I can read paragraphs 4, 5, and 6, which is Drenica. "Separately my defence attache reports that at approximately 1430 Zulu today, while travelling in Drenica with US and Dutch colleagues, he became caught up in an exchange of fire in the Josanica area in Drenica and close to the areas where the media claims the UCK to be organising. Special police were involved. At least 50 to 100 rounds were heard. DA reports that heavy weapons including the PRAGA air defence system were being moved into the area. DA and his travelling companions left the area safe and well. "DA has also reported that at around 1440 police were fired on at Kijevo between Pristina and Pec on the road that forms the southern border of Drenica. There are no details of casualties. "DA has also seen two platoons (approximately 60 men) of police (too dark to identify with certainty) including Jeep fitted with heavy machine-gun, moving west from Srbica towards Lausa. PJP units are still dug in around Prekaz." Can you, if you recall, mark on the map the area where this actually took place.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the area of the provincial town of Klina here. It was on the corridor that I mentioned to you earlier, stretching from the west from Decani through this area of Josanica to Klina and then the road that we were on was this area here, Josanica, which was close to a Serbian strong point with the KLA headquarters of Vojcnak, just there. And from Srbica, the element referred to in the last two platoons of Serbian police were probably a special unit by the JSO or the SAJ moving out of their headquarters in Srbica, which we latterly came to find out the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were the -- can you just -- you've just given two acronyms for two police units. Can you explain to the Judges what you're referring to when you refer to those. Who are the JSO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These, Your Honours, are the members of the Ministry of Interior, the MUP as they were referred to. The Special Forces, the SAJ and the JSO, were two counter-terrorist forces who were used for direct action operations and led most of the assaults within the province of Kosovo during 1998 and 1999. These are very well equipped, very heavily equipped, and designed to be the cutting edge of Serbian security activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 says that "police were fired on at Kijevo." And you've marked Kijevo. Where --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I haven't, actually, sir. Kijevo is in this area here, on the main road from Pec to Pristina. It is actually a -- and was an isolated Serb village that was held throughout 1998, 1999 as a flagship of the Serbs continuing to soldier and live on in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the police that were fired on in Kijevo, do you know who they were fired on by?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They -- it would be presumably elements of the KLA. As I've tried to indicate, the whole thing was a very muddled affair with people maintaining control over areas for a very short space of time, and then either side, either the Serbian security forces or the KLA backfilling in and causing trouble in the areas which had until recently been quiet. So it was a very fluid situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the -- in paragraph 4, the heavy weapons that are referred to. You refer to the PRAGA air defence system. What other heavy weapons did you see at the time that the Serbs had deployed into this area in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They had deployed PRAGA, which is an air defence system, and an armoured personnel carrier called a BOV-3, which again is a triple-barrelled weapon designed primarily for anti-aircraft use, and these, as I'm sure the court is well aware, are not designed to be fired at civilian folk, or military, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move to the next DipTel, which is dated the 25th of March, and it's behind tab 6, it's only paragraph 2. And this is now the day after your last report. You're still in Kosovo, it seems. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond "My DA reports the situation in the Lausa area, central Drenica, this morning as calm. According to Koha Ditore, an independent Kosovo Albanian newspaper, tracked police APCs were seen on the streets of Djakovica in south-west Kosovo near the border with Albania last night. They appeared to be heading out of town. Skirmishing apparently occurred throughout the night from Djakovica up round Decani to the Klina valley on the edge of Drenica. There are unconfirmed reports that at least four policemen have been killed (they were spotted in the Djakovica morgue). Five Albanians are reported killed, but the figure may well turn out to be higher. One Albanian compound in particular is reported to have been the focus of police operations." Now, this is an area that you've already marked on the map, but if you could just point Their Honours to the area that we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're dealing with the area in the west here, Decani, along this main road down to Djakovica, which was a principal town in the west of Serbia, quite a major town, along with Pec, and then into the Klina area, which is where I'm pointing now. And this is all, as I mentioned earlier, to do with the corridor that led from Tropolja over in Albania, over the mountains where the smuggling and other traditional routes which the KLA was starting to use as a resupply route into this area and particularly into the area of a little town called Junik which will be mentioned later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that skirmishing was going on throughout the night in the area you've just indicated. What do you mean by "skirmishing"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This would be light engagements, shots fired. This was to be synonymous with the way the campaign progressed, where, as I said, one side would make a play for a particular area, the other side would withdraw, and then under the cover of darkness they would come back in and take potshots at one another. So this would be going on in what I call a very fluid situation. So no side completely had control of the area. It was more who was in the more advantageous position controlled that area up until they decided to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, skirmishing between whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this particular skirmishing is indicated as going on throughout the night. Were you there during this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We were there in that area. We actually stayed in the town of Djakovica, down here. So we were very close to the area where this activity was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on to the next tab, which is behind 7. And this is a telegram dated the 26th of March of 1998. Now, is this a report which in fact is something that you would have drafted or provided most of the information for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I in fact drafted all of this for our ambassador, because it was based on my visual personal sightings, having now been in the area for nearly two months on a regular basis and therefore becoming extremely familiar with the area and with the, as I've said, the continuing changing fluid situation, but on touring on a regular daily basis all day every day, one got to know fairly well what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me just read parts of it. Paragraph 2: "Defence attache's assessment is that Serbian security forces now deployed and balanced to mount joint strike in Decani-Djakovica, and Drenica-Lausa-Vodnik areas." Now, without repeating ourselves again, those are the two areas that you've essentially already indicated to the Judges as to where military activity was taking place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 3: "Outline of forces: Show of overwhelming force: Outer ring: Capable of deploying 8.000 to 10.000 MUP - for urban deployment, crowd control - assisted by imported thugs. Smart cars seen from Ivangrad, Podgorica, Cetinje, Bijelo Polje, Novi Pazar, Belgrade, Kosovska Mitrovica, Ulcinj, Herceg Novi, and Urosevac. "(B) Inner cordon: 500-700 PJP holding inner ring of VCP's around operational area, supported by 10/15 APC's with heavy cannon. "(C) Assault force: Difficult to accurately assess, probably consists of SAJ (anti-terrorist unit) RDB/secret police, including helicopters Huey 212 direction finding equipment to locate UCK, Praga 30-millimetre cannon. Strength 200-400. Holding areas possibly Srbica ammunition factory, and area of Dobro Vodo. "Coordination and communication. Many incidents observed where news has not been passed to the next unit, indicating a fundamental lack of communication." Now, Mr. Crosland, just commenting on that. You're a professional soldier. What level of forces by this time were the Serbs deploying into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the Ministry of Interior side, as I've said, between 8 and 10.000 is probably a conservative estimate of uniform police, and as I've indicated, specialised police for using both as an inner cordon, what I would call grunt infantry, barely policemen. These are heavily armed individuals who were used for the assault led by a specialised assault force of the two forces we already talked about, the JSO and the SAJ, along with the RDB and the very effective Serb electronic warfare communications unit that were used against the Kosovo Liberation Army. That in itself is a substantial force in what is a very small area, bearing in mind that the whole area from Pristina to Pec and north to south is about 120 kilometres square. So we're not talking about a great deal of country. That is purely on the Ministry of Interior side. On the Vojska Jugoslavije, the Army of Yugoslavia side, you had stationed in the province of Kosovo, commanded by 3rd army at Nis, the 5th Pristina 52 Corps, which had three brigades, and additional forces were brought in. So you had in effect something in the region of in excess of 25 to 30.000 armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you state in the report that there were problems with communications between these units. Why did you make that observation in paragraph 3(d)?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Initially there was not over-good communication between the Ministry of Interior forces who were taking the brunt of the action and the Vojska Jugoslavije, the Army of Yugoslavia. This improved later on with a coordination cell based in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not going to read it but you make, in paragraph (e), some observations about their tactics, about Serbian tactics of these units that you've referred to. Can you explain the comments that are contained in paragraph (e) of this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The VCP, or vehicle checkpoint positions, were a tactic that the Serbian security forces used to drop off men at various strategic points around an area like in the Drenica, and it would be penny-packeting forces all the way around in an attempt to control the area. The major problem, and it was a continuing problem for the Serbians, that they failed to patrol out from these bases and therefore there was little if any control over and above what they could see, and at night, of course, it gets dark and therefore they didn't see very much at all. So in effect they had a lot of men in the area, but they were really controlling very little of a tactical or strategic nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say at the end of paragraph 4: "At present MUP/PJP have upper hand and therefore would be tempted to snuff out UCK by heavy-handed operations. UCK currently not being over-clever and need to fade into background. Authorities able to use overwhelming force to attempt to crush UCK and may well do so shortly, as the logistic and administrative problems build." What were the logistic and administrative problems that you're referring to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army in the first assault on them in the Drenica had decided to stand and fight and were summarily taken down by overwhelming force by the Serbian security forces. I think they began to realise that this was a mistake. The area, the whole area of Kosovo, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond majority of it, is rolling upland and downland, not conducive to a shoot and scoop principle, but very suitable for Serbian forces to use heavy armament over long range and therefore distancing themselves from the Kosovo Liberation Army, who at this particular time were not heavily resupplied or reinforced from Albania, and therefore relying on what forces they had in country at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next tab, which is tab 8. And this is a DipTel of the 7th of April, and I'm only interested here in the security situation, your paragraph, and I'll read it. "The security situation seems calm. DA visited Kosovo on 5 April and reported a degree of normality returning in some areas, although all police points remain manned. PJP were still in evidence. Large security force movements were reported around Podujevo and Srbica on 6th April though these may have been no more than normal rotations. Six bodies were found in a forest near Orahovac on 6th April. One plausible explanation is that these were Albanians loyal to the Serbian regime killed by the KLA, but no one has claimed responsibility." Can you just point out again for us, please, Mr. Crosland, the location of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, Podujevo is up here and is on the route going out of Pristina to the north and back towards Nis. It was the main supply route, or MSR as we call it, for 52 Pristina Corps to be resupplied from Nis, the army headquarters that was controlling this particular operation. And therefore they were quite rightly ensuring their lines of communication were clear and able to resupply their growing mounting of troops and police in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the six bodies that were found in a forest near Orahovac on the 6th of April, do you know anything about that event?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, we were called to Orahovac, which is a town in the middle here, it is actually the centre of the Bajrak and brewing industry and therefore extremely popular with everyone concerned. Mainly an Albanian town with Serbian businesses in it as well, and throughout the conflict the attitude of most of the businessmen there was that they would wish to get on with making money and distilling their wine and brandy and for everyone to take their grubby little fight elsewhere. So it is highly likely that these gentlemen concerned were killed because they were not helping the Albanian cause at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see the bodies yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We did see the bodies, but there was really no conclusive evidence as to how they came there and who had shot whom. This is all part of I said the fluid situation that prevailed throughout 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next tab, which is tab 9, and this is a diplomatic telegram dated 15 April, 1998, and the only two paragraphs I'm interested here, again in your section, the security situation, are paragraphs 2 and 4. Paragraph 2: "A police station in the Vranjevac suburb of Pristina was attacked late on 13 April; one policeman was wounded and the building was substantially damaged. There has been no formal admission of responsibility. There have been no reports of other noteworthy incidents, though Albanians report continuing harassment by the security services, and there are regular reports of gunfire in rural areas. Defence attache in Slinn (first secretary) are visiting Kosovo today and tomorrow." And then paragraph 4: "The state media is reporting that Serb families are leaving the Decani area in large numbers as a result of threats from armed Albanians. The reports are colourful and almost certainly exaggerated, but there is more than a grain of truth in them. Some 18 Serb families left Decani on 14 April, and the atmosphere among Serbs is becoming more tense. Some of our Belgrade contacts with connections to Kosovo admit privately that the remaining Serbs are thinking hard about their future. Even Papovic, no surrender, rector of Pristina university, has apparently bought himself a large flat in Belgrade." Now, Mr. Crosland, Vranjevac is a suburb of Pristina; that's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, and as in all of our countries, police stations are designed to be in amongst the public in order to administer law and order and therefore are not designed as tactical buildings. They are overlooked and extremely easy to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this a Serb area or an Albanian area of Pristina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was a mixed area, as most of the major towns in Kosovo were up until this period. And therefore, the police, the MUP, were going about their normal business of defending the local public, who would be both persuasions, either Serb -- Kosovo Serb or Kosovo Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the policeman a Serb or an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see the building? Did you see the damage to it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I've seen that building on many occasions. I don't particularly remember the damage at this time but, as I've indicated, it's a very soft, easy target, and no doubt this policeman was just doing his normal job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you find out at any stage who attacked it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, we didn't. At least, I don't think we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report, that paragraph goes on to speak of Albanians complaining about continuing harassment by security services and regular reports of gunfire in rural areas. Can you make any comment on that statement? Can you add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was a regular occurrence throughout 1998 and 1999 where both sides in what I call, again, a fluid situation, would fire at one another. The Serbians had defensive positions all around the -- their areas. And they would take appropriate action if they thought they were being attacked. I mean, it was an extremely jumpy time for everyone concerned, and therefore you would get outbreaks of gunfire, sometimes heavy, sometimes single shots, as each side would have a go at the other side. So it's not frightfully tactical or professional, it was just the way of life that happened in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4 you refer to Serb families leaving the Decani area. Can you just point out for us again Decani on the map.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, Decani is over on the west here. It's the home of another Desoki [phoen] Decani, which is another one of the Serb historic sites, monasteries. And we made a special tour up into the mountains here, which is quite high mountains bordering Albania, and in that area in particular there were a lot of Kosovo Serbs who had been there on subsistent farming, a very harsh regime, who felt that they needed to move out of the area which was becoming more and more safe. Due to activities on both sides, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "activities on both sides," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: There would be harassing by the Kosovo Liberation Army, and also the Serb security forces, in military terms, wished to have this area what they called a free fire zone so they would fire into it at will if they thought there was a target that required attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're pointing to the area around Junik on the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, to the west of Junik, yeah. Junik was to become a major point, a battle, later on in the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can go to the next, which is 21 April. And this is behind tab 10. And the only paragraph that I'm interested in here is paragraph 5, under security, and I'll read it. "During the night of 15/16 April, the Yugoslav Army intercepted a group of men apparently smuggling weapons across the FRY-Albanian border. Press reports suggest a convoy of eight horses carrying 12 boxes of arms and ammunition. There are conflicting reports about the number of casualties from the ensuing exchange of fire. Otherwise, there appears to be no change since my last situation report, sitrep." Mr. Crosland, first of all, do you remember this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As I say, it is part of a growing problem in the western province along the Albanian border here where the Serbs, and in particular in the area of Pastrik mountain here, were mounting, and quite Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond rightly so, operations to protect their own international border from intervention from Albania, and this was one of several occurrences where Albanian personnel in that context were caught on the border trying to come into the -- into Yugoslavia illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next tab, which is tab 11. And this is a diplomatic telegram dated the 23rd of April. And again I'll read it into the record, paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5. "The atmosphere in Decani and Djakovica remains extremely tense following the incidents yesterday afternoon and evening reported in TUR. This morning's press and the contacts which First Secretary has had in Kosovo (including Serbs, Albanians, and foreign journalists) confirm that there has been substantial shooting in the area and that many civilians, both Serbs and Albanians, have left the worst affected areas. There are various stories of Albanians abducting Serbs, of Albanians attacking VJ positions and of (from Albanian sources) of Serb forces attacking Albanian-inhabited villages. There are far more references to VJ involvement or at least presence from both Serb and Albanian sources than on any previous occasion since the crisis began. One report suggests that two Albanians were killed following an attack on a VJ installation. If this is true, it would be the first such attack on the VJ installation -- on the VJ and could provide a grounds for VJ intervention based on their stated policy. Sekulic (Jovanovic's chef de cabinet) has not reverted following my warning last night. "A respected local independent news agency suggests that the security force's attention has turned decisively towards Decani and away from Drenica, claiming that even the checkpoints leading to Donji Prekaz (the site of the first major incident of the crisis) have been abandoned. Although the state news agency Tanjug reported an attack by Albanians on Serb-owned houses in Crmljane village (in Decani) on the evening of 21 April, the state media has not so far given much attention to the incident. "Although so far the casualty figures do not suggest that a major clash has occurred, general deterioration in the situation has led to a number of attacks on journalists and other outsiders. The First Secretary has learned that the local interpreters working for the daily telegraph and ECMM were attacked by Serb refugees; the police intervened to rescue the ECMM employee following journalists' and NGOs' report that both Serb police and Albanians stopping vehicles have adopted a significantly more aggressive manner than hitherto." Paragraph 5: "It is difficult to assess immediate prospects, but there is strong local expectations on the part of both Serbs and Albanians (including some of our more reliable contacts) that there will be major clashes in the next few days. DA left Belgrade at 0430 this morning and should be in a position to report from the area by 1000Z, (communications permitting)." Mr. Crosland, the report refers to activities shifting away from the Drenica area to Decani. Can you just show us on the map what is meant by that, where military activity was shifting to at this time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This I think encapsulates what I said, it was a very fluid situation, flowing backwards and forwards from just west of Pristina in the Drenica, where the initial engagement was, to now a slightly more stabilised -- or less stabilised area in the west here between the towns of Pec, Decani, and Djakovica. And this was in response to, as I say, growing intervention in the means of resupply from and across the international border between Albania up through Tropolja and Bajram Curi into the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, you say that it was in response. Who was responding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The Serbian security forces were and remained extremely perturbed about the almost sieve-like area in the border through which the Albanians were attempting to reinforce a rather beleaguered, at this point, Kosovo Liberation Army within Kosovo province.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report refers to stories of Albanians abducting Serbs, of Albanians attacking VJ positions, of Serb forces attacking Albanian-inhabited villages. Did you see any evidence of that when you went down there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we toured on a daily -- almost daily basis into the area, remaining overnight either in Pec, Djakovica, or in Pristina, or in Prizren down in the south-west here, and therefore became extremely familiar with the modus operandi of both the Serbian security forces and also the Kosovo Liberation Army. And as I said, both sides had the habit of attempting to gain the upper hand albeit it for however short a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you refer in this report to the involvement of the VJ, of the Yugoslav army. Why was particular reference made to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, within the Yugoslav constitution, the Vojska Jugoslavije, the army of Yugoslavia was primarily tasked for the defence of the international borders of the former state of Yugoslavia. They were allowed to operate initially to within -- to outside of 500 metres. This then was enlarged to two kilometres and eventually enlarged to 20 kilometres. And later on, in about July of the -- this year, they were entrusted with the job of trying to maintain the lines of communication, the four major routes through -- from Pristina to the western side of Kosovo. So that was a major change in the application of military force, which up to that point had primarily been the repertoire of the Ministry of Interior police and the various associated special units, which we've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So up until this time, the Yugoslav army had not been directly involved in conflict within Kosovo itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They had -- that's not quite correct, sir. They had been involved on the border, particularly on the western side here where they had deployed extra units outside of the organisation of battle of the 3rd army out of Nis. This was elements of the 63rd parachute brigade, the 72nd special forces brigade, and coming in shortly would be the 1st Armoured Brigade from Belgrade to reinforce the elements already within the boundaries of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report refers to a number of attacks on journalists and other outsiders at this time. Who was carrying out those attacks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I said, the whole thing was extremely fluid, and I think people arrive on these roads, some of which were dirt tracked, to fairly isolated positions of both the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, on the Serbian side; and the Kosovo Liberation Army; and quite naturally people opened fire at vehicles because there had been vehicle-borne attacks against both sides. So it was an extremely difficult and slightly dangerous job to wander around to get the information. But this was a fact of life that everyone had to take into account. And I'm afraid -- I think some journalists were with their journalistic zeal to find out what was going on had a rather nasty surprise on occasions. I don't think there was anything particularly vitriolic about it; it was just a fact of life that everyone in the area was rather frightened and feared for their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You predict in paragraph 5 that there would be major clashes within the next few days after this report on the 23rd of April. And why were you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, we were starting to see a considerable build-up of both Ministry of Interior forces, a movement as we've indicated already towards the western side of Kosovo to try and close the border there, which was becoming a major thorn in the Yugoslav security side. And also, as was indicated, the Vojska Jugoslavije might be taking a more personal interest in what was going on around the area for their own security.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can go to the next tab behind tab 12. And this is a DipTel of 24 April, 1998. And I'm interested here in paragraphs 2, 3, and 5, and I'll read them. "The VJ has stated that they have taken action to deal with infiltration of the FRY/Albanian border by a group of 200 terrorists in an operation which began on 22 April in the Djakovica area. At least Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond 16 "terrorists" killed. All the evidence suggests that the operation was well-planned and based on intelligence. This morning's press (headlines including "war on the border") describe an ongoing operation. There are reports that there may already be significantly more casualties. One report, for which we have some collateral, suggests that the FRY authorities have intelligence suggesting that as many as 1.000 more terrorists may be preparing to cross the border. We have been told by western journalists that the KLA effectively control security in Kuksi, Albania. It appears that civilians have largely evacuated the affected border villages. "As discussed with the department, my telecons with Phillips EAD, both I and DA sought to raise last night with appropriate contacts our concerns that a major operation was in train. None of our usually cooperative interlocutors were available. I therefore sent a note to the MFA and FMOD at 2230 Zulu last night expressing our concern (text by fax to EAD). The MFA is holding a briefing for ambassadors" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "The MFA briefing at least appears to have been planned yesterday afternoon, which may suggest that the government was even then expecting to have to justify a major operation. (Although it could also have been planned to follow up on yesterday's referendum, either to gloat over the 75 per cent turnout and 97 per cent no vote so far estimated, or to present a new initiative). In either case, the government, which has already summoned the Albanian charge to complain about the incursions, is likely to call again for international action to protect its border with Albania." Paragraph 5: "My" -- I'm not going to read the first sentence. The second sentence: "My DA's assessment is that the VJ have been faced with a serious challenge to the FRY/Albanian border of which they had some advance warning but for which they are woefully unproposed. They are genuinely afraid of losing control of significant parts of Kosovo, particularly if (as it appears) the KLA strategy is to link Drenica and Decani, the two areas in which the Serbs have least control." Mr. Crosland, do you recall this operation taking place for the 24th of April of 1998, on the border? We're talking now about the border operation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do. And as part of -- as I initially said, my job was to interface at the very highest level with the Vojska Jugoslavije, to which I was accredited only not to the MUP, Ministry of Interior. And I received a briefing from the chief of intelligence, General Dimitrejvic as to this operation itself. And it appeared -- and as it appeared in later times that the Yugoslav forces had very good intelligence about the Kosovo Liberation/Albanian support in bases or towns like Tropolja and Bajram Curi and that they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point to those again or can you mark them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Tropolja is here, over in the border of Albania, and Bajram Curi is further back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you mark Kuksi.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Kuksi is this village, this town down here which is on the major road into the south-western province of Kosovo crossing at Vrbnica which is one of major international crossing points which led up to the western town of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report states that western journalists were stating that the KLA effectively controlled security in Kuksi. Do you know whether that is correct or false?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: From the information I received from the elements within the Vojska Jugoslavije, that was their impression, that the Albanian authorities had more or less given up an attempt to control that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, over the page at paragraph 5 you say that the Yugoslav security forces, the VJ, were woefully unprepared for this border incursion. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: On this particular occasion they had good intelligence and they planned a major ambush against this incursion, which had been relatively successful, because the Albanian reinforcements had walked up more or less a track straight into a Vojska Jugoslavije ambush position and had suffered accordingly. What, of course, the problem was or then happened was that the Albanians got slightly cleverer and decided to move around these static locations, which only controlled the immediate area where the Serb security forces had a presence, which is what I had been alluding to all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So that when you say they're woefully unprepared, you're suggesting because of these static positions they couldn't actually control access over the border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. They manned specific border positions, some of which I went up to visit and saw. And it was quite clear that they were not overkeen on venturing outside these defensive areas, and particularly during the hours of darkness which was used by the Albanian insurgents to move men and equipment across.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the final sentence you say: "They are genuinely afraid of losing control of significant parts of Kosovo, particularly if, as it appears, the KLA strategy is to link Drenica and Decani, the two areas in which the Serbs have least control." Now, who was afraid of losing control?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The -- Your Honours, the statement that kept on coming from the Vojska Jugoslavije, the VJ general staff in Belgrade, was that the Albanian border was a completely open border which was being vagrantly infiltrated by Albanian elements in support of the Kosovo Liberation Army. And that if the international community was not prepared to try and attempt to seal this border from the Albanian side, then the Serbs would have to sit and wait until people crossed the international border and then attempt to deal with them. And as I've indicated, that was fine if the Albanian insurgents appeared in front of prepared VJ and MUP ambush positions, but if they decided to go higher or lower on less used and less regular paths, then their chances of getting through with whatever equipment, men, and ammunition was reasonably good. I mean, it's a very difficult border to police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you say finally in that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Particularly when - sorry - on the Albanian side there was a complete breakdown of law and order as we had seen the year before when Albania imploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you're talking about the Republic of Albania now itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say finally: "Particularly if, as it appears, the KLA strategy is to link Drenica and Decani, the two areas in which the Serbs have least control." Now, that's a comment in the report. Is that something that you believe the KLA strategy was at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do. As I said already, the corridor of influence from Albania through the western area or province of Kosovo into the area which was called Jablanica and then up onto the Drenica area was the major corridor of influence and where we initially came into contact with some of the major KLA headquarters involved in this -- these particular incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether that's an appropriate time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the first break now, resuming at five minutes after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are now 28th of April, Mr. Crosland, and only another six months to go. This is the DipTel behind tab 13, telegram 281, and I'll Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond read paragraphs 3, 4, 5, and 6, and I've been asked to slow down. "My DA has been touring Kosovo today and reports that the situation in Decani is notably more tense than recently, with few civilians in evidence. Although the towns of Djakovica and Pec were relatively calm, some explosions could be heard from Djakovica. He has been unable to confirm the Albanian reports that some villages have been attacked with heavy artillery. Police checkpoints have been reinforced (with regular policemen) and the mood is decidedly more jumpy. DA remains of the opinion that the special police are still operating in the area, though it is difficult to provide hard (and publishable) evidence for this. The army (VJ) are much in evidence with increased numbers of men and materiel being moved by road. While travelling through Srbica (Drenica), DA was again stopped by armed Albanians. The clear impression is that the Albanians ("KLA" or whoever effectively control this - and perhaps other - areas." Just to break it up, Mr. Crosland, and if we can deal with this paragraph first. Can you just indicate on the map the area, first of all, that's referred to, Djakovica and Pec, just if you could point them out to us again.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're dealing with the western side of the province of Kosovo. Pec in the north, the major town; Decani in the middle here; and then Djakovica in the south. And it was along this line and in particular this major road, Tarmac road, that the Serbs were trying to prevent Albanian infiltration into the rest of -- the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report the army are much in evidence with increased numbers of men and materiel being moved by road. What, if any, was the significance of that at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It really confirmed that the Vojska Jugoslavije was now fairly fully engaged in supporting the Ministry of Interior operations, and in the area of Decani we did in fact come across a six-gun battery artillery position. But as was indicated in paragraph 3, Albanians had indicated that artillery was being fired against the border areas. And this was confirmed by myself as we drove through the entire position. And this is the first time that we'd actually seen the Vojska Jugoslavije, and in particular the artillery being used in combined operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say combined operations, you're referring to the police essentially, with the police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. They were providing the indirect and direct fire support with artillery to operations that were ongoing in the area as we alluded to before the break, which are of a very fluid nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say in the report that while travelling through Srbica you were stopped by armed Albanians and your impression was that the KLA or whoever effectively controlled this and perhaps other areas. Can you point out the area of Srbica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Srbica, Your Honours, is in the area here of the Drenica, which is where the first major incursion took place in 1998. And as I said, it was cleared on about three or four occasions by the Serbian security forces and then infiltrated or backfilled by the Kosovo Liberation Army on a regular basis. One lot would move out and the other lot would move in. So who controlled it at which time was extremely difficult to ascertain. And only by touring on a daily basis throughout the area did you get some idea of who was potentially in charge of which area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say at this time, on the 28th of April, you had an impression that the KLA was controlling it. Why did you get this impression?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because more or less in this area instead of Ministry of Interior troops had now been taken over by regular bands of KLA. At this particular point the Kosovo Liberation Army, or UCK, were short of a regular dress uniform throughout their forces. So you would have in some areas armed civilians, armed with the same weapons as those people, both men and women who were dressed in military uniform of varying natures. So there was no regular KLA uniform at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on to paragraph 4. "In DA's absence, staff sergeant attended a second briefing for the attache corps given by Colonel General Dimitrejvic. The objective was clearly to present the FRY/VJ side's position on recent events in advance of the 29 April Contact Group meeting. He gave a detailed account of recent incidents (verbatim record by fax to EAD and MOD). His conclusion was that the Albanian authorities were actively encouraging and arming the terrorists. He added that the FRY Security Service had identified a training camp at Tropolja; they had the names of some 2.000 to 2.500 men who had been trained at the camp." Now, Mr. Crosland, this was a briefing that took place in Belgrade by Dimitrejvic to the defence attache group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the fact that -- the facts I'm interested in here, first of all were you aware at any point independently of this, that there was a training camp at Tropolja?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was aware from various intelligence sources that information had been received that there were training camps over in Albania, as I've indicated already, in the area of Tropolja and Bajram Curi and down at Kuksi as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just point those out again because I --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. In the area of Tropolja, which they talked about in this particular report, also Bajram Curi, and then down further south in the area of Kuksi which has been mentioned on the main international crossing point at Vrbnica into the province Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And as far as you had been told, who was being trained in these camps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As far as I was told by Dimitrejvic and outside intelligence as I received in the course of my duties, these were Albanians, also from the diaspora, the various countries in which Albanians had gone to, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just finally, paragraph 5: "Dimitrejvic stressed that the VJ had a responsibility to protect the FRY border and would continue to take the necessary steps to do so, but there now were no VJ units in Kosovo other than those regularly based there, i.e., the Pristina Corps and the VJ had no plans for a wider operation. It was essential for the international community to press the Albanians to abandon terrorism before they launched the major attack for which they appeared to have been preparing." What VJ units was Dimitrejvic referring to in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: General Dimitrejvic was referring that within the province of Kosovo the 52 Corps was the major army unit there and that there were no other reinforcements. I think this is probably a slightly moot point. I think he's trying to put across that the Vojska Jugoslavije was able to just about hold the border and that the situation was reasonable. I think in his own heart he knew that the situation was a lot worse than he alluded to, but he reinforces the point that unless the Albanian border was properly policed on the Albanian side, then there would be -- there would continue to be incidents along this international border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, he states that unless some kind of action was taken, there was going to be a major attack. Unless the Albanians were pressed to abandon terrorism, there was going to be a major attack. Who was going to be launching a major attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
