utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, that General Dimitrejvic is referring to what I've already insinuated, that because this international border was so poorly policed on the Albanian side, there could well be another major attempt to infiltrate - as on the previous one nearly 1.000 people of which I think 200 were killed - across this border, and therefore the Vojska Jugoslavije would be extremely pressed to maintain their own border intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So an attack by whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: An attack mounted across the Albanian/Yugoslav border by Albanian insurgents, which was on an illegal basis. This is an international border not being properly policed by the Albanian authorities. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can go to the next report, which is behind tab 14. And this is a diplomatic telegram of the 30th of April, 1998, and here I'm interested in paragraphs 3 and 5. "The KLA issued a nine-point statement on 29 April, published in Bujku, the mass circulation radically-inclined Albanian-language Pristina newspaper, saying that the homeland was in a state of war and was fighting to liberate and unify Albania's occupied territories. The statement called on Albania to review its stand. It was the duty of the free part of the homeland to help the occupied part. The KLA was ready to strike against the enemy at the right time. However, the KLA was ready to take part in talks with the enemy, but only after the occupying troops had left and with the mediation of a third party. Any agreement without its presence would be invalid. The statement appealed to the frustrated and faint-hearted who were trying to plunge the people into defeatism and anarchy who were trying to remove themselves from the scene." Mr. Crosland, just specifically referring to the statement that the homeland was in a state of war and was fighting to liberate and unify Albania's occupied territories, did you ever while you were there at the time come across those kinds of statements from KLA members that you met?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. All the time was the view put forward by the KLA and other personnel, that this was a mission to re-take what was called by the Serbs Velika Albania, Greater Albania, which included the province of Kosovo. I think, if I may, we have to remember that in a census in 1991 there were well over two million Albanians already in the state of -- the province of Kosovo, and that the, if I may use an English phrase, the minority or the goldfish in the bowl were actually the Serbs and not the Albanians. And although the Serbs technically controlled the government, the Ministry of the Interior, police, the MUP and obviously the army, the VJ, major wealth was actually exercised by the Albanian businessmen and farmers who had left Albania under Rugova in order to get a better life in the southern province of Serbia called Kosovo. So it was looked on by the more radical elements of which the KLA was obviously the leading edge. This was the aim of the KLA, to move wholeheartedly into this area, which has been an area of, throughout history, which has been fought over, and depending on which map you go to, it depends on which side of the border, Albania or Serbia or Kosovo, it appears in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 of the diplomatic telegram: "Rumours continue to circulate in Pristina about the fate of a group of Serbs apparently being held hostage by the KLA. It is thought that around a dozen Serbs (comment: Not clear whether civilians or security forces) have been captured in separate incidents over the last week. Serbian organisations were trying on 29 April to enlist the help of an international NGO to negotiate their release. Some international journalists have been told by a radically-inclined Albanian human rights organisation that some of the Albanians killed in the 23 April border incident were mutilated when handed back to their families for burial. There are reports that an Albanian was shot dead by the Serbian police while on his way to attend the funerals of the Albanians killed near Decani on 27 April. A policeman was reportedly killed in an attack on a police patrol on the Prizren-Urosevac road late last night." Now, Mr. Crosland, do you recall around the 30th of April hearing rumours or facts about Serbs being held hostage by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And throughout the conflict in 1998 and 1999, we estimated that probably about 200 Serbs had been taken -- captured by the Albanian forces, for want of a better term. This particular incident was never completely proved as far as I'm -- I was aware. It happened in a place called Blace, which is in the middle of this area south of Komorane and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you mark that on the map, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The actual town, the actual area itself is not marked, but it's somewhere down south of Komorane, over here, an it's south of that area, towards Sedlare. This area, Sedlare, was a UCK base, headquarters. But it was an allegation from the Serbs, and I think, to be honest, a very fair allegation that many Serbian people disappeared into -- mainly into this area south of Pec in an area called Ljubanica [phoen] and were held prisoner there and most of them disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this report also refers to an Albanian killed in the 23 April border incident being mutilated when handed back to families for burial. Do you know whether that was a true allegation or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I didn't specifically see this particular mutilation. I did however, Your Honours, see, unfortunately, many others, and reports are made to that effect. But this was a -- I'm afraid, a sad occurrence that took place on a fairly regular basis as a way of -- I suppose of trying to frighten, terrorise, the other side into submission, and is a peculiar, nasty habit of the Balkans area, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report also refers to an Albanian being shot by the Serbian police near Decani, the 27th of April. Was that incident reported to you while you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mean, these incidents, as I've indicated, were happening on more or less a daily basis, because all along, the western road here from Djakovica through Decani up to Pec, there were many Albanian -- or mainly Albanian villages and Serbian isolated villages. And if people needed to go about their lawful business and they walked into a position of either Serbian or Albanian, the chances are after dark they may well be killed because of a nervous nature of both sides being isolated and frightened out in this country.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Finally, you refer to a policeman being killed in an attack on a police patrol in the Prizren-Urosevac road. Can you point out that road for us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is the southern route down from Prizren here in the west, up to Srbica, which is a Serbian community, and on into Urosevac, which was again a mixed town of both Albanian and Serbian origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you move the map across a little, please. Can you mark Urosevac for us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, Urosevac is in this area here, or now it's called Ferisaj by the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall this event being reported to you, this police officer being --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not specifically, no, but as I've indicated, Your Honours, this was happening on a -- sadly, on a rather daily -- daily basis. So individual attacks like this were just yet more of the casualties on both sides, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next tab, at 15. This is a report of the 5th of May, and I'll read paragraphs 1, 2, 3, and 4. "Reports of heavy fighting in Ponosevac, near Albanian border. UNHCR estimate 5.000 refugees have fled Montenegro since crisis began. LDK spokesman backtracks on Rugova's welcoming of the contact group's measures. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Ivanov to see Milosevic today. Albanian foreign minister warns of risks of war. "Both sides report heavy fighting around or in Ponosevac, around eight kilometres from the Albanian border, near Decani. What is not clear is who initiated the violence, which apparently began on 3 May. Initial reports spoke of several Serb police wounded by Albanians. Fighting has continued since, with reports of Albanian casualties and a further build-up of Serb police forces in the area. MUP forces were extremely tense when DA and First Secretary visited town on 2 May. Albanian sources claim that foreign media and humanitarian workers have since been denied access to the area. "There have also been reports of several clashes in villages in Drenica. Details are hard to confirm, but there appear to have been casualties. The Yugoslav army has also said that it successfully drove back armed Albanian groups attempting to enter FRY on 2 and 3 May. No report of casualties yet. "DA touring the area over the weekend found very heavy MUP and VJ deployments. Most worryingly he saw 80/100 of the special anti--terrorist police, (JSO) in four separate locations (these are elite troops of the state security and rarely seen). He also confirmed PJP and MUP Special Police co-located with Yugoslav army in Pec barracks. He will be visiting again today." If we could have the map up, please, and if, Mr. Crosland, you could point out to us the location of Ponosevac where this fighting was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is the area of Ponosevac, which leads directly up to a major crossing point oppose Tropolja, at the Morines pass or Morines Col. That was both a Vojska Jugoslavije position and a MUP position, with artillery and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What fighting was taking place there at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In this area there is a, leading out of Djakovica, south of Djakovica, there is a dirt road that leads around to Ponosevac, Brovina, Batusa, and up to Junik, and then back on to the main road. And this was becoming a front line area in which all the villages had been -- or villagers had been cleaned out of their area and sent packing as the thing said, the report said, mainly to Montenegro. And the -- on the Serbian side they were attempting to clear the area so that they could use it as a free-fire zone, and the Albanians were attempting to use the area to infiltrate across the border. So the whole area was extremely tense. Any livestock in the area had been shot. Most houses had been very badly damaged, and the civilian population, as I said, had virtually been driven out completely of the whole area. So the only people in there were either Serbian security forces or Albanians attempting to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this fighting in this area commenced on the 3rd of May of 1998 and was now in its third day. Is that fair to say from this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in this same report there were also reports of fighting in the Drenica area, and I know I've asked you to do this before, but if you can just indicate to the Judges what area we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back into the initial area here from Srbica -- or from Gornji Klina down through Srbica down to Komorane. So as I said earlier to Your Honours that one set of forces would move out, the other would move in and so the situation would change sometimes on an hourly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then you refer in paragraph 3 that the Yugoslav army had stated that it had driven back Albanian groups attempting to enter the FRY on 2 and 3 May. Is that the matter that you've just been referring to that was taking place around Ponosevac in the early part of May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct. It is -- also leads up to the pass at Col Morines where there was another VJ deployment up on the border and there had been several reports of an attempt by Albanians to cross in the vicinity of this Vojska Jugoslavije position unsuccessfully. Information was extremely difficult to get by because to get up there was virtually impossible. It was sealed off and some of the tracks were even mined which made vehicle access impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You also make the point in the last paragraph, in paragraph 4, that you saw 80 to 100 special anti-terrorist police in four separate locations and also PJP police co-located with the Yugoslav army in Pec barracks. Why were you were worried about seeing JSO special anti-terrorist police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These police, as I have indicated, Your Honours, are the best trained and the best equipped and also the personnel that were used to carry out the strike of operations. We found bases in Pec itself and out at a place called Istok or Dubrove [phoen] as it's sometimes referred to, in Pec. There was a combined Vojska Jugoslavije and MUP barracks on the road leading south out of Pec towards Decani. There was JSO based in Decani itself where the artillery unit had been found, and there was JSO based in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why were you worried? Why did you describe it as worrying to see these particular types of troops?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think it indicates just how seriously Vojska Jugoslavije was taking -- or the Yugoslav authorities were taking it, and they were prepared to meet force with appropriate force, if required.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what force were they confronting at this time, the security -- the Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As indicated, Your Honours, in the report there were infringements of the Albanian/Yugoslav border, not quite on a daily basis but certainly on a weekly basis. And reports were building up from other intelligence that I was privy to, that more and more Albanian personnel were moving back to Albania to listen to the call of arms to follow the KLA into Kosovo. And also at this time in May, in early May, the conditions on the mountains were now -- the snow had melted and so conditions on crossing these fairly high mountains were not so difficult as they were in the severe winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it says at the beginning of the report that the Albanian foreign minister at this time had warned of the risk of war. Do you recall that warning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. And I think it is all part of the Yugoslav pressure to -- for the international community to do something about the international border between Albania and Yugoslavia that was not, as I've repeated many times, was not being properly policed on the Albanian side. And therefore we were getting these intrusions illegally across an international border of armed men and horses, camels, whatever -- not camels, sorry, donkeys, carrying ammunition and other stores into the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the Albanian foreign minister was warning of war between who?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Potentially between Albania, I suppose, and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next tab, which is tab 16. I think this actually simply gives more detail of what we've previously discussed. I'll read it and then I'll ask you if you have anything to add. Is this the report that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a report of the 13th of May of 1998, Kosovo situation report as at 11/12 May 1998. Summary. 1: "Situation in Ponosevac area very tense. Area of Ponosevac, Djakovica, Pec, and Decani patrolled by elements of JSO and PJP in a very heavy-handed way. Villagers have fled north to Junik. Main road Pristina-Pec still closed between Komorane and Kijevo VCP's. Drenica quiet, VJ deployments around all major garrison towns. "Ponosevac. Road from south to Ponosevac 'carpeted' in empty cases including 40-millimetre grenades. Villages south of Ponosevac deserted, livestock slaughtered in fields, houses sprayed with gunfire. Ponosevac empty except for JSO/PJP, who are carrying out patrols from Decani using APCs, including TAB C 79 and IPR, similar to M-60. Most villagers now concentrated in Junik, about 3.000 with enough food and water but no telephone. "Comment. This JSO/PJP operation is perhaps to freeze this unknown transit route and cut off supplies to the UCK in Jablanica. "MUP. Strength generally increased, particularly in the west region. All other VCP's as normal, but increase in deployment of APC's. Number of MUP seen, approximately 400 plus or minus, APC's 26. "6 times BOV-M were seen heading south on Autoput from Belgrade over weekend 9/10 May. "Pec-Pristina road. Open to traffic from Pec to Klina. However from Kijevo VCP to Komorane still closed due to sporadic firing. Very little traffic seen. "Drenica area. This area is quiet and fairly relaxed including the Lausa area, now the only road access through. "VJ. VJ deployments still around garrison towns as last reported but as yet not further involved. "Assessment. Situation could rapidly spin out of control, post-ongoing talks if Serbian security forces feel that they are losing control. Heavy-handed terror action in Ponosevac area indicates that the tactical thought process has not changed." What is the heavy-handed terror action that you're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think in paragraph 2 in the Ponosevac paragraph where I say "carpeted in empty cases," this road which I've indicated to you before on the west here from south of Djakovica round through Ponosevac, this whole area was deserted apart from military folk. Any living animal had been killed. Most, if not all, houses were now in a very bad state of disrepair, having been fired at continuously by Serb security forces. And it was just indicative of we were forced to put people out of their houses to flee to where they could find safety. And in this case most went north towards Montenegro, but not all. Some went west into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that the Pristina-Pec road was closed between Komorane and Kijevo. Why was that and can you indicate that road to us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the main road here is from Pristina all the way across here to Pec. As I indicated earlier, there are four roads that cross this area, one from Kosovska Mitrovica in the north, through Rudnik, along to Pec. The one in the middle from Pristina to Pec itself. From Pristina south to Stimlje, over through Dulje, Suva Reka, down to Prizren. And by this stage these three routes had more or less been closed by the KLA with very minor positions on these roads. And most of the Vojska Jugoslavije traffic was now coming south to Urosevac and then up over the mountains into Prizren. And this route was allowed to be kept over for resupply purposes. I think it was just indicative of the KLA trying to increase their authority over areas of Kosovo by claiming they blocked the major routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically with the Pristina-Pec road where it was closed between Komorane and Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It was closed at a place called Lapusnik, which is just west of Komorane, which is here, and Lapusnik, another village where the mountainous area met this main road where the KLA put in a blockade with light defensive positions around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the assessment that you made is that the situation again could rapidly spin out of control if the Serbian security forces feel they are losing control. Why did you say that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've indicated, the area in the west here, the road south of Djakovica through Ponosevac and up to Junik are mainly -- or most of the villages from Pec down to Decani and back down to Djakovica were all deserted and extremely badly damaged. And so the indication was that the Serbian tactical thought process was: We'll blitzkrieg the area and drive the civilian population out of it in an attempt to try and control or militarily control the area by fear rather than by any proper strategic thought. And in that fact they succeeded in driving the civilian population out of the area, but that did not necessarily mean, as I've said many times, that they controlled the area. They really controlled the areas just around the defended areas that they had all along these routes, as I've indicated, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And who at this time controlled the areas outside these major defended routes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I've indicated, Your Honours, it was a very fluid situation. Out of sight of the Serbian positions, the KLA would walk around and move men and equipment through and continue as they had done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, which is a report actually of the Pristina Corps, the VJ Pristina Corps, to the command of the 3rd army. And it's signed by General Pavkovic. And in paragraph 1 he gives an assessment and proposal for the engagement of the Pristina Corps. This is a document, actually, that can be made public, but I will just read some paragraphs, Mr. Crosland, that I want to draw your attention to to ask you some questions about. The second paragraph of paragraph 1: "The security situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija is getting more complex every day due to the operations of Siptar, derogatory term for Albanian terrorists, whose increasingly frequent attacks on MUP members citizens of Serbian nationality, and Siptars loyal to the system are sowing fear and uncertainty. "The basic aim of Siptar terrorists in this phase is to take control of extensive territory in Kosovo and Metohija, and to create a Liberation Army, which for the international community would represent a legitimate popular army, not a terrorist organisation. "With the aim in mind, they are working on increasing their numbers which they achieve by voluntary recruitment, and by methods of threats and blackmail. In this way, the terrorist organisation has managed in relatively short time to mobilise respectable forces, numbering at this moment between 3.500 and 4.500 men armed and trained for armed raids and guerrilla operations. "By their manner of operation and application of intelligence and security, engineering and logistics support measures, the terrorist forces are increasingly taking on the attributes of a military organisation and are setting up units from platoon to company size. "The command cadre consists of former JNA officers of Siptar nationality, a number of officers from the Croatian and Muslim armies, and mercenaries from the Republic of Albania. "The terrorist organisation's members' morale and resolve for armed resistance has lately been on the rise, due to the inefficiency of the MUP and its poorly executed operations aimed at destroying terrorist nuclei." Let's just talk about those paragraphs. Did you know General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I did, Your Honours, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had you met him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I met him on several occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just in respect of each of these paragraphs, do you think -- was it your assessment that the aim of the Siptar terrorists was to take control of extensive territory in Kosovo and Metohija and create a liberation army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said already, Your Honours, this appeared to be the long-term aim from what had been in the early 1997 and in 1998 a fledgling liberation army, which was now beginning to gain some apparently international credibility. And as I said earlier, the idea of Greater Albania, which included -- or they hoped to include the province of Kosovo. I think the numbers that General Pavkovic replies to is a very debatable area. I myself had said that I thought there were between 400 and 500 what I would call hardcore KLA. It is difficult to say who is correct. If he is taking into account the potential numbers that were apparently and possibly training in Albania itself, then those numbers are 3.500 to 4.500 are not too far-fetched.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of the organisation taking on attributes of a military organisation at this time by setting up platoons, companies, did you observe that at this time at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think it's with respect, Your Honours, very difficult to look at a terrorist organisation in the same light as regular forces who are based on specific organisation of platoon, i.e., 30 persons to a company of 100 to a battalion or a regiment of between 400 and 600 men. I personally visited about five or six KLA headquarter bases scattered throughout Kosovo during my time there. And I would say at this stage in May they were not as organised as General Pavkovic is saying. I mean, he may have been using this for his own propaganda, and any general facing an insurgency as this was is bound to put a more glossy view on the opposition in order to ensure that he gets the correct support to deal with the problem that was a very real problem and a growing problem. But to say that it was as organised within platoon and company, you know, 30- and 100-man units, I think it was possibly stretching the credibility at this particular time. There was a basic area of command and control, but I stress basic, and that was basically against mainly linear - either a road or a river - into which that area a headman would have what I would best describe token authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were officers from the Croatian and Muslim armies within the KLA? Did you come across that at all as Pavkovic is suggesting here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. As the former Chief of Staff and now currently in Kosovo is General Agim Ceku who was Croatian, ex-Croatian. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Ceku was a KLA member?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, he also states that the terrorist organisation members' morale and resolve for armed resistance has been on the rise due to the inefficiency of the MUP and its poorly executed operations aimed at destroying terrorist nuclei. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I think it is. And it's in the way that the MUP operations were carried out. As I've tried to indicate that villages would be -- they would probably get on to the talk either local radio, warn a village that they were going to shell it, fire in a few shells to just chivvy the local population out, and then raze that particular village. This doesn't do a great deal for the efficiency or the morale of either the civilian population or the military concerned because they walk into an empty village and wonder what they are doing. And immediately you are driving or potentially driving civilian population who may actually be pro your operations against you. So this was a counter-productive but very typical of all the fracas that have gone on in the Balkans where the civilian population has generally taken a hammering from whichever side happens to have the biggest gun in its hand at that particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you go over the page, Mr. Crosland. In the first paragraph he simply emphasises what you just said, that the MUP forces had been unable to destroy terrorist nuclei in Drenica, so we'll move on from that. He then states that: "In our estimate, the terrorist forces currently hold about 30 per cent of Kosovo-Metohija territory. They have succeeded in putting under their control the Kosovska-Mitrovica-Pec and Pristina-Pec roads, as well as the local roads of the areas of Drenica, Decani, and Djakovica." How would you assess the truth of that statement by Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've indicated to you on the map, the top three roads from across from Mitrovica to Pec and from Pristina to Pec and from Pristina through Stimlje and down through Suva Reka and on to Prizren all three -- top two were closed by the KLA. The third one was ambushed on a regular basis by the KLA, which increased the difficulty of the MUP and the VJ forces resupplying their own positions. And I think, if I may say so, this is General Pavkovic having a go at the MUP who up until that time had primacy in operations. And it was about in this time, if I remember correctly, that a more coordinated response was put into action by General Pavkovic and the various MUP authorities in Pristina to try and attempt to bring together the two operations. And this, as I've said before, involved the VJ in operations outside of their initial constitution in defending their own borders to now being used in measures across and throughout the province of Kosovo in order to maintain lines of communication and defence of significant Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who had the upper hand at this time, the Serb security forces or the KLA at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honours, it's difficult to say who had the upper hand. The -- as General Pavkovic has said, for the KLA to tentatively hold, in parentheses, 30 per cent of the area is quite significant for still very much a fledgling liberation army. On sheer numbers, the Serbian security forces had more men available for military operations. It's a question of whether they could be properly and wisely used and effectively used against the liberation army, but it learnt its lesson and was not prepared to stand and fight but to drift away into the shadows, to come back and fight another day. A very difficult operation to achieve by regular forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you're saying a very difficult operation to achieve by regular forces here, you're referring to the Serbian forces actually dealing with the KLA tactics at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct. In -- because of the modus operandi of shelling an area, driving people out, obviously no one stayed there, so no people were killed. So people drifted off to fight another day, and a lot of ammunition was expended, and not a great deal of people were killed fortunately, but did they achieve militarily what the Serbian forces wanted to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on in fact to the next document, which is tab 18. And this is a DipTel of the 14th of May of 1998, and here I'm interested exclusively in paragraph 6. "Security situation. Today's press reports an attack by 50 armed Albanians on a Serb community near Klina. One policeman was wounded. If true, this represents another ratcheting up of the scale of UCK actions. Official Serb sources claim that ten Albanians were killed at Smonica near the FRY/Albanian border after mishandling launcher grenades. Albanian sources, however, claim that the ten were killed by land mines. Today's 'Dnevni Telegraf,' considered close to the security services claims that Stanisic, head of the secret services and Milosevic's advisor on security, has been put formally in charge of police operations in Kosovo. My DA is touring Kosovo today." Can you point Klina out for us on the map.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Klina is a small town on the -- one of the main roads and is on what I've refer to as the corridor from the west through Decani, Jablanica, into Klina. And then the road from Klina going eastward goes up through Josanica into Srbica into the Drenica. So it was a road that was both patrolled by the KLA and had static positions by the Serbian security forces. This particular attack I didn't -- I was not present at, but it is typical of what was going on in that Klina was a joint Serbian and Albanian town. Again, a police station in the middle of the town to do what policemen normally do, to look after the civilian population, and therefore it was a soft target and an easy one for the KLA to have a crack at.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document behind tab 19. This is a diplomatic telegram of 15th May, 1998. And just paragraph 8 I'm interested in here, Mr. Crosland, and I'll just read it to you. "My DA has reported in detail to Ministry of Defence on his tour of 14 May. MUP operations were ongoing in Djakovica and Ponosevac. Special police (of all varieties) were much in evidence, though there were no signs of VJ activity outside the border areas. DA and his colleagues were briefly detained by KLA, and it is evident that the KLA effectively control parts of Drenica and probably other areas too." So now we're at the 15th of May, and I know it's somewhat repetitious but it's the nature of the chronology that we're going through. Can you point to Djakovica and Ponosevac again.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- the area we've been talking about, Djakovica here, Ponosevac, Junik. There was very heavy fighting throughout this area because the KLA had made a stand or attempted stand in the town of Junik, and this was yet to draw the full fury of the Serbian security forces which happened later on. But it's indicative of the ongoing heavy conflict that was going on in this area throughout this middle part of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report says that you were briefly detained in May at this time by the KLA. Do you recall where that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We had driven towards Klina, which I indicated to you just recently, and then we had taken the route out up towards Josanica, past a Serb position, and then we were detained just south of Vojcnak in towards Lausa which was still held by the Kosovo Liberation Army, and that's where we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long were you detained for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think probably about 45 minutes. And I think it may be in this time that we went to a further KLA headquarters at Vojcnak, which is north, where I'm indicating on the map, just slightly west of the main Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you say that it was evident that the KLA at this time is effectively controlling parts of Drenica and probably other areas, too?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because on driving through this area there was again the KLA had taken over the positions of what had been formally MUP positions and were more in evidence than the Serbian security forces in this area. So it was part of this seesaw performance that went on all year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we go to the next report, which is 27 May, so 12 days later than the prior report. And I'm interested here in paragraphs 8 and 9. "The security situation appears to have deteriorated sharply in recent days. There have been reports, including from British journalists, of heavy fighting in Decani and Drenica. There are regular Albanian claims of massacres and attacks on villages. The security forces issue frequent reports of attacks on police patrols, including two kidnappings of Serbian policemen since the weekend. There is talk of a KLA "prison camp" near Glogovac. Although these stories are impossible to substantiate and there is a heavy element of propaganda and sensationalism on both sides, the overall impression is that the violence is spreading as both the security forces and KLA try to assert their control over the strategically important corridor between Drenica and Decani. The security forces seem to be particularly active in the area around the villages of Jablanica and Gllodjan, believed to be important KLA headquarters. "On 26 May, acting DA saw 11 MUP coaches, 30 heavy lorries, and special place (JSO) vehicles towing artillery pieces travelling down the main road from Pristina to Pec. This may reflect normal rotation, but even so, it indicates a very heavy MUP presence in the area. "On 27 May, he saw burned and badly damaged houses north of Drenica. Local eyewitnesses' descriptions were consistent with JSO operations. Access to the whole western area was heavily restricted. In addition, new MUP checkpoints have been set up in south-east Kosovo around Urosevac and Gnjilane. First secretary counted eight on 24th May. Stojilkovic, Serbian minister of interior, said on the 26th of May that the police in Kosovo would operate more efficiently, given his reputation. This is a worrying sign in itself. There are also claims in the press that Arkan's paramilitary forces are active in Kosovo. ECMM recently encountered a group they were told worked for Arkan. For their part, the KLA have set up their own checkpoints on main roads, one just two kilometres from an MUP point. Separately, reports continue of lorries travelling to Kosovo being stopped and of humanitarian assistance being hijacked." Now, in terms of the first paragraph, Mr. Crosland, paragraph 8, heavy fighting in Decani and Drenica, again I know it's sort of 12 days after the prior incidents, but what can you comment on what was taking place on the 27th of May in these two areas that you've already referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, it just indicates that these, the two -- perceived to be the two critical areas from both sides. The Drenica was historically an Albanian area of interest, and Decani is of interest I've indicated is close to the Albanian border, there which their resupply and reinforcements were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whose resupply and reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the camp, the KLA prison camp near Glogovac, did you hear of these rumours yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And we attempted to get near this place in Glogovac, which is just north of Komorane. It's an old mining area, which was subsequently used later by the Serbs as also a potential prison camp. But as of the context here, it was impossible to substantiate either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any further comments on paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: For the first time, really, the majority of the fighting had taken place on a line from Podujevo through Pristina down to Urosevac. Giljane is in fact east of this, and that was the first time that we'd had inference that there was potential KLA activity in the east of this area. So that in itself was possibly a significant factor in that the KLA authority was starting to spread to Giljane, which was again a heavy populated country town with both Albanian and Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it on the map, Giljane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It is not. If you look at Urosevac and follow this road, another couple of inches or so, 40 kilometres, you'll come to that town, which houses both a Vojska Jugoslavije brigade and had a heavy Albanian population itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can go to the next. This is a diplomatic telegram of the 29th of May. Paragraph 3. "Incidents continue. Movement remains restricted. The situation in and around Decani, where fighting has apparently continued for four days, is still confused. The Belgrade press continue to claim that the KLA is besieging the town and express shock that this has been allowed to happen. Albanian sources claim that hundreds of Albanians dare not leave their homes for fear of being shot by Serbs still controlling the centre of the town and that there is no food. Some reports talk of fighting in the streets of the town. If or when the media regain access, the pictures of damage and destruction could, regardless of which side is responsible, prove emotive. "The local branch of the radically-inclined council for the defence of human rights and freedom have launched an appeal for international humanitarian assistance for Decani. They claim the situation is further complicated by the flow to the area around the town of several thousand "refugees" from villages closer to border looking for security. "There appear to have been several fresh attacks on the police checkpoint at Komorane, 21 kilometres west of Pristina on the road to Pec, and further clashes at Slatina, close to Pristina airport, 12 kilometres from the town. Albanian sources claim that three people died and another wounded in an instant near Orahovac when a car was shot at by police". Here again, Mr. Crosland, can you just again on the map point to the area or the town of Decani?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, Decani is here and then the area of Junik, which as I said earlier was becoming the focus of intense Albanian and Serb activity as to who was to get control of this small town. And as I said earlier again, the border area was becoming an increasingly difficult area for whether Serb or Albanian villagers to live in. Most of the Serbs had moved up to the Rugova pass area, and Albanians had fled into Montenegro and also into -- west into Albania. But again, it's just highlighting the fact that this was becoming the key area for control of resupply from Albania into Kosovo and for the Serbs to mount some kind of halt to this illegal activity across an international border. The other attacks refer to the major road out of Pristina to the Komorane crossroads, which if you recall, was blocked by the KLA at Lapusnik. At Komorane there was a fairly heavy block, or police checkpoint, but again being a static point was open season -- is now quite midsummer, nights are drawing out, so people would go around and have a pot at the policemen as part of the active night's activities. Slatina is closer in and is in the area called Veliki Slatina which is a MUP outpost guarding the road that goes south towards Pristina airport, which obviously was a key Serbian Yugoslav airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So fighting was moving close to Pristina at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I think it's indicative of, again, static Serbian positions being attacked. And we will see them coming even closer to Pristina in the continuing months.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want to take a break at this point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be a convenient time. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could turn to tab 22. The only paragraph that I'm interested in here -- first of all, this is a regular operations report to the third army command in the military district command in Pristina. I know you've referred to this already, but what was the third army command again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the third army was -- headquarters was in Nis which is outside of Pristina. And they are commanded by General Pavkovic, and the forward formation was the 52nd Corps based in Pristina which was doing the current operations within the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the third army was the superior headquarters for the forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Nis is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what is this document? This is a report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This is a report by the staff officer in Pristina dealing with, by the looks of it, day-to-day operations and reports of those operations which were coming back into -- from Pristina to the senior headquarters back in Nis as a situation report of what is going on in the operational area and is a standard format for reporting events back to the higher authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just read here. "On the morning of the 8th of June," and this is para 8, "Albanian thieves attacked the villages of Suvo Grlo and Banje, Srbica municipality. These are Serbian-populated villages, whose inhabitants put up resistance on their own." If we could now -- we'll come back to this, but if we could go to the next report, which is at the 9th of June. This is a diplomatic telegram, as I say dated 9th of June, 1998, and going to the security paragraph, which is paragraph 5. "General situation seems calmer, although reports from Albanian sources of shelling and air attacks on villages close to the FRY/Albanian border, especially in the Djakovica area. A VJ soldier was killed and three others wounded in attack nearer the village of Popovac near Djakovica. Armed Albanians have attacked the last two Serb villages in the Drenica valley, Banje, and Suvo Grlo. The and of fire is said to have lasted several hours. This is the apparently third such recent attack. There are also reports of sporadic gunfire from the Komorane police checkpoint 20 kilometres west of Pristina." Now, the two villages you refer to are in fact the two villages that Colonel Maksimovic refers to in his report to the third army command, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They are indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know where those two villages are in Drenica? Have you been able to find them on the map?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, they are not actually on the map because they are two very small villages. But they are in -- this is referring to a situation that starts to develop closer towards Pristina to the Belacevac mine, which I'm sure Mr. Cayley will come on to later on. This is an indication of the spreading out from the Drenica, which is this valley here, as I've indicated to you on several occasions. We're now starting to threaten the capital of Pristina from the Drenica valley. The other valley -- the other town mentioned of Popovac near Djakovica, again is not on this map but was four or five kilometres out from Djakovica towards Zrze on the road going south towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was -- were in fact the -- you were aware personally that the villages of Banje and Suvo Grlo had been attacked at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware that there had been instances in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And equally the village of Popovac near Djakovica, did you -- were you personally aware that a soldier was killed and three others wounded in an attack near to that village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm not personally aware of that particular instant, no. But I have no reason to doubt the validity of this particular report because it, as I've mentioned many times, the situation was changing on an hourly basis and from day-to-day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again this report refers to gunfire at the Komorane police checkpoint. Can you just point that out for us? I know you've already --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Komorane is here at the bottom of the Drenica valley and was the major checkpoint guarding the route going back into Pristina and Slatina where the Pristina airfield is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can now move on to the next document, and this is a report of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade to the command of the Pristina Corps. What was the 243rd Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this brigade was based in Prizren on the map, as I indicate here, and had the task of holding open the road from Prizren up through Suva Reka to a place called Dulje, Blace where the Vojska Jugoslavije had a command group of about 200 or 300 men deployed including artillery and armoured personnel vehicles. And then with help from Vojska Jugoslavije units from Urosevac, keeping the road open through Crnoljevo which was a K -- Kosovo Liberation Army base or headquarters, down to Stimlje and then the road up to Lipljan and on up to Pristina or south to Urosevac. It was a joint Vojska Jugoslavije operation to keep that route open and on which they suffered a fair number of casualties from ambushing in an area which was both mountainous and heavily wooded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll just read parts of this report. Paragraph 1. "At 1035 hours on 14th June, the DTG sabotage group opened fire from automatic weapons from the direction of Luznica village at [illegible] ground. The place and the distance from which fire was opened was not determined [illegible] there were no consequences for the unit. "At 1110 hours on the same day a reconnaissance patrol which was reconnoitring Dulje-Luznica village was ambushed in the sector of trig point 925 where two soldiers were lightly wounded. It was retaliated [illegible] and the reconnaissance patrol pulled out of combat. Wounded soldiers were sent to Urosevac for treatment. "At 1235 hours on the same day in the Crnoljevo sector, near the restaurant, a regular supply column of BG-243 combat group came under attack. Three soldiers were seriously wounded and one received light injuries. They were transported to the Pristina medical centre for treatment." Paragraph (a), at the bottom, 2(a): "Losses in manpower: Seriously wounded troops in the Crnoljevo village sector: Zeljko Antovic, son of Vojislav; Veroljub Smiljkovic, son of Momir; and Stojan, son of Mitar. Soldier Vojislav Vasic, son of Zivadinka, was lightly wounded. Soldiers who were lightly wounded in the Dulje pass sector. Bogdanovic and Slobodan Jokic, son of Vukasin." Now, I know, Mr. Crosland, you don't specifically know these events that were reported here, but can you say anything about this report, bearing in mind what you've said about the area of defence of the 243rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The validity of these reports are entirely in line with what was going on in that area. As I've said, it's a very difficult and demanding road which goes through the mountainous area from Stimlje to Dulje to Suva Reka and down to Prizren. The road was open to attack and ambush at many points on the road and that brigade suffered many casualties. I think a later report indicates that we actually went to help several of the Vojska Jugoslavije who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can go to tab 25. 16 June, 1998, a report from military district command Pristina to the 3rd army command. And paragraph 8. "Situation report on the territory: At the send-off of recruit Srecko Mihajlovic, Dobrosebina village, Zubin Potok municipality, the recruit's uncle involuntarily shot the recruit in the leg, causing him an entry-and-exit wound. Siptar, derogatory term for Albanian separatists, attacked a MUP, Ministry of the Interior, patrol near Rakovina village on the Djakovica-Klina road. One policeman was killed and two were wounded. A VJ Yugoslav army column transporting food was attacked on the Urosevac-Stimlje road. Two soldiers and a civilian were wounded. An IP reconnaissance patrol was attacked in the surroundings of Juznice, Suva Reka municipality. Two soldiers were killed." Again, Mr. Crosland, I know you're not aware specifically of these events, but what does this report demonstrate in light of what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The first part of the report refers to the village of Rakovina here, which is in the middle of the area here and where there was -- both an MUP and then later on a Vojska Jugoslavije deployment all the way down the eastern side of this higher ground which was in position to try and keep an eye on the -- what was called the Jablanica area to the west of the river. And this -- this whole area was subject to sporadic attack by KLA throughout the rest of the year because they again were static military positions which offered targets to the KLA fighters on a regular basis. So these reports are typical of the ongoing attrition that was being taken by the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the column travelling on the Urosevac-Stimlje road where two soldiers and a civilian were wounded.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Again, on the map Urosevac is here, and Stimlje is here, and this was a supply from Urosevac which was a main -- another brigade deployment for the Vojska Jugoslavije going forward to a forward base at Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether there were -- were you aware of any attacks on that road by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: During the -- there were a number of attacks on that road which was again a very easy road to attack because of the countryside being fairly heavily wooded around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document which is dated the 18th of July -- June of 1998. And this is another regular operative report to the 3rd army command from again Lieutenant Colonel Dragoslav Maksimovic. Paragraph 8. "Between 1000 and 1100 hours Siptar, derogatory term for Albanian, outlaw gangs from the village of Crkvena Vodica, Obilic municipality, abducted Milorad Spasic, father of Zivko Spasic, who had been abducted a month ago and so far there has been no information about him. "Milorad Spasic's brother had been abducted this morning in the village of Crkvena Vodica, Obilic municipality. "After 1200 hours today, at the Belacevac strip mine, Siptar terrorists hijacked a Gaz motor vehicle with five people, of which three were Siptars, and they were released immediately. The other two were Serbs, and they were held together with the vehicle. One of the two Serbs is Predrag Milic from Plemetina village, and the name of the other is not known. "The situation in Stimlje municipality is very complex after a soldier and a policeman were killed in Crnoljevo yesterday. Last night after the killing of the soldier and policeman, a group of Serbs broke the window of Siptar shops. Fearing a direct conflict with Siptars, most Serbs have evacuated women and children and so only men fit for military service remained in Stimlje." Now, specifically in terms of the Belacevec strip mine, were you aware of that particular attack by the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We knew that the situation around the Belacevac mine, which is a prestigious mine in Serb terms, had taken place. This is a pretty unpleasant area under the shadow of the mine with sulfur and all sorts of other unfortunate ingredients in the air, a mine -- a place where -- mainly inhabited by Serbs who worked in the mine and were now being attacked out of Drenica valley by elements of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point out where the mine is located.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Just in this area here, about 10 kilometres from Pristina itself. Obilic is just to the north, which I'm now indicating on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In terms of these abductions, you were not specifically aware of these individuals being abducted, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not of the individuals, no. But we heard reports that these isolated Serbian homesteads had been attacked and possibly people were being taken prisoner. It was not confirmed as such. But it was I suppose a terror tactic by the Kosovo Liberation Army to further increase their authority over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the next page it says: "The situation in Stimlje municipality is very complex after a soldier and a policemen were killed in Crnoljevo." And I know you've pointed out Crnoljevo on a number of occasions, but were you ever aware of members of the Serb security forces being killed in that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on several occasions, Your Honours. Because, as I indicated, Stimlje was the forward potion prior to going up the road to Crnoljevo, which was a KLA headquarters which we visited and was therefore the object of sporadic attack by the KLA as and when they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, which is tab 27. This is a diplomatic telegram of the 19th of June of 1998. Paragraphs 3 and 4. I'll read it. "Both Serb and Albanian sources report a number of new incidents. Reports suggest that up to three policemen may have been killed in clashes on 18 June. "An official press release states that on the evening of 17 June, a group of armed Albanians attempted to cross the FRY/Macedonian border near the guard post at Djeneral Jankovic. When the Albanians refused to stop, the border guards opened fire forcing the group to return into Macedonia. The report states that weapons and ammunition were found at the site that followed the Albanians retreat." Now, do you know where that border crossing is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If you look at the map, it's the major border crossing on the route -- it's the major route that goes from Pristina south to Skopje in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you move the map up -- sorry. Oh, thank you. And you've marked it there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this was the first time that there was indication of an allied effort of support from Macedonia for the KLA, Kosovo Liberation Army, coming from that area. And there were to be several scattered incidents to the west of Djeneral Jankovic along this very difficult area to patrol, again a mountainous area on the northern or northern border between Macedonia and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you specifically recall this particular incident when there was this incursion across the Macedonian/Yugoslav border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Because it -- as I said, it was an indication that the problem was spreading not just from the Albanian side now but potentially from the Macedonian side as well, and therefore was a significant incident to have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next report of the 20th of June. This is an interim report to the 3rd army command from the military district command in Pristina. "Two Serbs were abducted in Jelenac village, Klina municipality, between 1300 and 1400 hours today. "The abduction took place in the tilled field by the house. Drago Vostanic, son of Trajko, born 1931, and Radomir Vostanic, son of Milutin, born 1928. "Three Dobric families were expelled from the Veliki Djurdjevak village. Klina municipality. "Serbs are leaving the village of Dusevic, Klina municipality, under pressure by Albanian terrorists. "Terrorists are fortifying positions along the Pec-Pristina road above the Drsnik village, Klina municipality. "At the approach to the village of Stepenica, Klina municipality, Albanian terrorists blocked the road with logs." Can you point out for us again the -- if Jelenac is on there? It may not be; it may only be Klina.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not, Your Honours. We're dealing with the area between Pec and Klina here which was -- this road was continually under attack and clearance by both sides respectively. And these villages were in north and just to the south of that particular road itself. So these are opportune targets. Both sides are attempting to influence the area by forcing or trying to abduct personnel from either Serbian or Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you weren't aware of these specific individuals, but were you aware in that area of abductions of Serbs taking place and Serbs being forced out of villages in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Again, these were very isolated villages which the Serbs attempted to remain in and which were then attacked by the KLA in order to abduct Serbs on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you have no reason to believe that this report is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. It's a report that we often came across in our daily dealings with the MUP on these roads who stopped us and informed us about what was going on. So I don't have any problem with this particular report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We could now go to the next document, tab 29. This is a diplomatic telegram dated 23 June 1998. And I'm going to read most of it. "KLA may now control as much as 35 per cent of Kosovo and is able to act in around 65 per cent. Even less moderate Albanians fear that it is beyond political control. "In a changing situation, in which - despite the new freedom of access - some parts remain out of bounds for security reasons, we cannot be sure how much of Kosovo is under KLA control or, perhaps more importantly, how much is not properly under FRY/Serb control. But a rough guess would be that the KLA actually controls some 35 per cent of the province and now have the capacity to mount attacks anywhere west of Pristina, i.e., in around 65 per cent of the province. The MUP has abandoned most checkpoints on the roads bordering the Drenica triangle, large parts of which are clearly now under KLA control. Glogovac and Srbica are the only towns where there appear to be residual Serbian presence. Malisevo and Lapusnik in central Kosovo appear to have fallen to the KLA." Let's, just to break it up, Mr. Crosland, deal with it paragraph by paragraph. At this time, on the 23rd of June of 1998, the embassy was reporting that the KLA controlled 35 per cent of the province and was able to act in 65 per cent of the province. Was that something that you were reporting to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is correct. And I think there was a general feeling within the embassy that the situation was getting into a very serious stage. And the percentage figures there are indicative of what we have been talking about, but as I've reinforced to you continually that the idea of control is perhaps too strong a word for it, because it flowed backwards and forwards. But at this particular stage, those percentages are not -- are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report states that Malisevo and Lapusnik appear to have fallen to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just point to those two places. I know you've marked them already.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Lapusnik is here on the main road from Pristina to Pec. And then Malisevo, which was in fact one of the major headquarters of the KLA is between -- come down the road from Lapusnik through Crni Lug to Malisevo and on to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the report states that at this point the MUP had abandoned most checkpoints on the roads bordering the Drenica triangle. What area are we speaking of there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We're talking about the area from Gornji Klina to -- through Srbica down to Kluvanje [phoen], and then along to Klina and back up to Djurakovac, up here in the north, and round to Rudnik. So it is a big area that they were trying to -- attempting to control, and I think at this particular point, if I remember rightly, they were attempting to run out their MUP personnel through the area and therefore had to release temporary control of this area back to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 5. "Significantly KLA attacks appear to be moving ever closer to Pristina, Kosovo Polje, five kilometres from the capital is perhaps the closest." Now, I know you've already referred to this, but can you make any further comment on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I mentioned to Your Honours before, the area around the Belacevac mine and the Serbian villages there that came under threat, Kosovo Polje again is a very emotive area, being the place of the monument to the battle of Kosovo Polje, and therefore an attempt to -- I suppose to dislodge the Serbian thought they could control this area of Kosovo by attacking one of their sacred monuments, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 and 7, tactics. "The KLA's approach seems to have been to wrest control of the main roads by first taking strategic villages off the road. Two of the three main east/west roads are now closed. If the KLA do not move to close the third between Pristina and Prizren, it will almost certainly be because they have chosen not to do so rather than because they cannot. It is striking that so far three other main roads remain unaffected: Those from Pristina to Podujevo, Mitrovica and Urosevac. All three are Kosovo's major links with the outside." Is that something you had reported to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. This report is actually by the deputy head of mission. What he is saying is that - and quite correctly - that the three roads across Kosovo were far more easily able to be closed because the country lent itself to them, to being closed and being ambushed. The roads from Pristina to Podujevo north was a major road which was attacked from time to time but was relatively easy to keep open. The road up towards Mitrovica in the north here, again, went through primarily a Serbian area because of the mines in Kosovska Mitrovica. And the major roads south, from Pristina down to Urosevac, the country was much more open and therefore very much more difficult for insurgent forces to ambush and hold a main road like that because they were totally without cover against a very mobile and aggressive Serbian force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 7. "At the same time, the KLA move into villages, initially in order to help defend against Serb attacks, but then leave a small party behind once the security forces have left in order to secure the village for the KLA. Some Albanians are now prepared to admit that the KLA has ordered that at least some of the refugee evacuations, partly for presentational reasons, in order to blame the Serbs, but also partly to clear the territory for fighting." Now, again, you've already pointed out that this was reported by the deputy ambassador, but can you make any comment on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, it is perfectly true. Both sides were attempting to influence the international community to back their own respective causes. And it was quite clear that the KLA was operating in this area; I saw it on many occasions and had people talk to me that they had been ordered out by the KLA in order to then try and bring in the international community to show them that they had been chased out by the Serbs. So it was a very confused situation, both sides struggling to achieve international recognition, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next tab. This is diplomatic telegram dated 24th June, 1998. We've already referred to this event, but I will read paragraph 8. "Both Albanian and Serb sources are reporting that the KLA has taken control of a coal mine in the village of Belacevac, just 10 kilometres west of Pristina. Shooting could apparently be heard in the area all day. Albanian residents of the village are reported to have fled to Pristina. KLA is claiming control of most villages in the area. The KLA has issued an appeal to local people not to abandon their homes. The KLA will guarantee their security. Comment: If these reports are true, it represents further escalation in KLA activity, demonstrating (a) the KLA's ability and confidence to mount such an attack so close to Pristina; (b) the KLA's readiness to intimidate Serbs in their urban and semi-urban strongholds, which is likely to encourage them to leave; and (c) the selection of economic targets. There are several other mines and plants linked to the power industry in the area. The other major industrial complex in Kosova is Trepca near the northern town of Kovoska Mitroveca. There have been occasional reports of KLA attacks on buildings making up the Trepca complex, but as yet not of a substantial offensive. "Fighting apparently continues around Klina in western Kosovo. As ever, it is difficult to know exactly what is going on, but evidence suggests an attempt by the KLA to take control of some Serbian villages in the area and thus open up a corridor between Drenica and Decani. Around 800 Serbs are reported to have fled to Klina from neighbouring village. There are also reports of clashes around Decani, Prizren, Djakovica, and Stimlje." Now, you've already referred, Mr. Crosland, to the attack on Belacevac. Is this report an accurate reflection of what you remember stating at the time to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. This report is actually by the deputy head of mission. I would agree with most of the report. I think perhaps he's overstating the ability of the KLA to inflict quite such control. Quite rightly they had attacked the area around Belacevac and driven out Serbs from their -- these isolated villages in an attempt to destroy the economic welfare of the area, although that did not actually happen. Trepca up by Mitrovica is just off the map, and there is up here behind -- by Bradas, which is part of the top of this particular map, there was another KLA headquarters by Bajgori [phoen] which we went to visit, and they had been mounting attacks down onto the Trepca mine in order to disrupt Serbian activities in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 9, if you could just -- it refers to fighting again around Klina. Can you just point to us where Klina is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah. In the Klina area, in the centre here, it was on the main corridor as I've referred to frequently through western -- through Junik, Jablanica* to Klina, and on into the Drenica. So it was a critical area for the KLA to try and maintain a regular supply of men and munitions into the eastern area to try and reinforce the sporadic attacks - and I stress the sporadic attacks - around Belacevac and Trecka, which were isolated areas, but it was an attempt to spread their power and influence into Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The report states that 800 Serbs had fled from Klina to neighbouring villages. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I don't specifically recall that number, but travelling in that area and visiting these empty villages, it was clear that a lot of Serbs had moved out because the areas were no longer defendable. So the figure, I wouldn't necessarily disagree with that figure, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next report, 26th June, diplomatic telegram 26th June, 1998, paragraph 4. "According to official Serb sources, two Albanians were killed and six captured by the VJ following an attempt to cross the FRY/Albanian border north-west of Djakovica. Albanian reports claim that there has been further shelling in the border area. Armed Albanians, wearing KLA uniforms, are reported to have stopped a bus on the Prizren to Pristina road near the village of Crnoljevo between Stimlje and Suva Reka on 25th June, taking three Serbs hostage. Serb sources report that in total 33 Serbs have been kidnapped since late April and remain missing. DA is touring Kosovo today. "The Montenegrin Commissioner for Refugees has stated that there are now some 11.500 refugees from Kosovo formally registered in Montenegro. The Commissioner estimated that the actual total would be closer to 15.000. (Comment: Difficult to make an independent judgement, but the Montenegrin authorities might well have reason to exaggerate the figure)." Now, first of all, Mr. Crosland, in respect of the border incident at Djakovica, what can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I think this is indicative of the ongoing loose situation on the Albanian border where there was continual attempt to breach this border into Yugoslavia or into Kosovo. And on this particular occasion, these individuals were stopped and killed. And this was happening, as I said, on a fairly regular basis. As regards Crnoljevo, we've already gone over this particular area. It was a UCK -- a KLA headquarters, and therefore people going through that area were liable to be hijacked and used for KLA activity. And the Serb -- the total of 33 Serbs, as I've said, I think in October we estimated something like 200 Serbs were missing, presumed being been kidnapped by Albanian elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you -- just out of interest, do you recall this specific event on the 25th of June, of these Serbs being taken hostage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not this specific event, no. But it was an event that is perfectly credible and believable in that area because it was a no-go area. It was a very difficult road, easily ambushed, very close to a KLA activity area, and very believable. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph 5, the commissioner for refugees in Montenegro. What ethnicity were these refugees in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These would be Albanian, Kosovar Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why would the Montenegrins exaggerate the figures of Albanian refugees in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think partly to try and increase NGO activity into that area, to give them more funding. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Go to the next document, tab 32. This is a diplomatic telegram of the 30th of June, 1998. Go to security at the bottom of the first page and then Belacevac mine. Paragraph 5. "There are confusing reports about the outcome of yesterday's security force operation against the Belacevac coal mine. Some sources claim that police have recaptured the mine seized by the KLA last week and that it is now back in the hands of the power company. However, the usually reliable (Serb) Pristina Media Centre confirmed to us at 0930 Zulu that only part of the mine has been retaken. There are fresh reports of security force action in the area this morning. "We have obtained some further background. In yesterday's operation, police appear to have surrounded the area and then apparently used tear gas to flush out those occupying the buildings. Foreign journalists talk of armed Serb civilians participating in the operation. Some also mentioned VJ involvement. Automatic gunfire and explosions were heard in the area all day. Large numbers of people were seen leaving the area on foot. Because many were men they were thought to be Serb employees of the mine. There are no reports of casualties at the time, although Albanian sources are claiming that an 8-year-old boy died when security forces attacked a nearby village in the same operation. The Belgrade press is speculating about the beginning of a Serb counter-offensive." Now, Mr. Crosland, again I know you've already referred to this particular event, the Belacevac mine, but can you add anything to these paragraphs in respect of Belacevac itself in your memory of events at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not uncommon for armed Serb civilians to participate in guarding their property and their villages. And In respect of what was going on, I think if I had been in the same place I would have done the same thing. Not all the villages could be protected by Serbian security forces, and therefore they resorted to arming their civilians to allow them to try and stay within their homes. This Belacevac area was a classic case in point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The report mentions the VJ involvement in the re-taking of the mine. Were you aware that the VJ had been deployed to Belacevac of this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were. The Belacevac mine is one of the key Serbian work forces in the area, and therefore a prestigious target that they wished to regain, if you will, their rightful control of. I mean, it was not an Albanian thing; it was a Serbian-based industry. So they were really reclaiming what they rightfully thought as their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the final sentence talks about the Belgrade press speculating about the beginning of a Serb counter-offensive at this time. What is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
