utterances.text: I think, with respect, I think it's exactly what it says. There was a lot of speculation going on between foreign journalists who were starting to come into the area because it was starting to get an exciting area to be in, and the Belgrade press was always keen to tubthump that they were about to sort out the Albanian problem in Kosovo. And I think these reports were delivered as a way of I suppose maintaining Serbian morale as much as anything else. But at this point in time, the situation was slightly stalemated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Stalemated between whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Between the KLA and the Serbian forces for, you know, reasons I've already mentioned that Serbian forces were moving their troops in and out and therefore were not in a position to mount -- I think a counter-offensive is slightly strong language to be -- this is building up something that wasn't really quite there at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 7. "There have been no reports on the situation in Kijevo. Clashes in and around Djakovica and Decani seem to have continued, although at a lower intensity than on previous days. The Media Centre claim four Serbs were kidnapped from a bus between Prizren and Stimlje, bringing the total of Serbs kidnapped since the beginning of March to 40. (Comment: The fear of kidnapping is taking its toll on Serbs who are beginning to avoid travel around Kosovo). Serb sources also claim that there have been two further attacks on factories in Kosovska Mitrovica, where there are heavy Serb populations. (Comment: The aim seems to have been to intimidate Serbian workers into staying away, rather than to destroy the buildings)." Now, the clashes around Djakovica and Decani, is that essentially what you've previously referred to, the ongoing problems at the border area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a continuation of the problem that's been going on there now for nearly two months and indicative of the -- one of the key areas that both sides were striving to maintain their own majority in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the reports of kidnappings since the beginning of March now totalling 40, what comments do you have about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, it was an ongoing phenomena that in order to increase the fear in Serbs, they were being kidnapped on a relatively regular basis. I mean, it was difficult to travel around the area of Kosovo because of the heavy engagement of military forces of all shapes and sizes from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of these attacks at the factories of Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we were. And if anyone's seen those factories in Mitrovica, you wouldn't want to work in them anyway. So if it was made more unpleasant, they would leave. It's a particularly nasty area. It is also in the area where in Zvecan that Arkan's paramilitaries were based. And So it was an attempt again -- Mitrovica was a -- is a joint Serbian and Albanian town, and therefore again it was an attempt to undermine the very limited Serbian industry that is in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We could now not move on to the next document, but I'd like you to direct your mind and rely on your memory for a moment. You recall on the 1st of July of 1998 you went to Malisevo. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Yes. Sorry, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you go to Malisevo on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because I had had various indications that this was actually the major headquarters of the Kosovo Liberation Army, and therefore I decided to go and investigate and see whether this -- these reports were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just point -- I know you've probably pointed to it about a hundred times to Malisevo, but if you can just --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We came through Orahovac and there was a Vojska Jugoslavije position on the north edge of Orahovac, and then past that and literally on the next bend was a KLA checkpoint which then -- we were then led under armed guard into Malisevo where there were about 150 to 200 personnel in various forms of uniform, quite heavily armed. There were defensive positions of a very linear and simple instruction all the way from Orahovac north into Malisevo. And in the major crossroads in Malisevo, the KLA headquarters to which I was escorted was just above and to the north in a black and white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you -- you said -- how many personnel did you say that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Approximately 150 to 200 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Mainly light pistols and carbines and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you see in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Within the headquarters, there was at least one radio set, indicating that there were an ability to community. I'm not a signals expert, but I would suspect -- I suspected it was capable of communicating outside of Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did it look like a military headquarters to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, it was very similar to all the other headquarters that we'd been to. There was slightly more formality within this area, and slightly more, and a more so soldierly-like way of behaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anybody appear to be in charge? Was there a commander?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, there was a person in charge. I was not totally -- I think Krasniqi was there at one stage, and I'm not exactly certain who was the other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say a man called Krasniqi was there. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: At that time I think he was actually their finance person. And he added a modicum of sense to the meeting that was getting quite heated at one stage with them thinking of trying to abduct us, which I indicated was not -- I don't speak Albanian; I speak Serbian and German. So we were speaking in German, and I suggested this was not a good act to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the KLA in Malisevo threatened to abduct you and your party?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you say to them when they threatened to do this to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I said that as the defence attache to Yugoslavia, I was entitled to travel wherever I was allowed to. They disputed that, saying this was not a part of Yugoslavia, this was now a part of Albania under their command, to which I disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long were you held there for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We were held for about an hour and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that there was an individual who appeared to be -- there was a person in charge. Why did you think this person was in charge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Because as I've said, he put on or he controlled what was getting a rather heated discussion as what they were going to do with myself and my party and added a bit of sense to what was otherwise becoming a rather pointless argument as to who was in control of which part and which part of the country we were currently in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of what he was called, the commander?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The name Celiku has come up. I'm not completely convinced if that was him or not, and it would be difficult for me to say under oath whether that was the exact name or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The commander, this individual who you saw at Malisevo, did you have any idea of what area this individual commanded around Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We knew from other intelligence that this area was potentially at that moment the major headquarters, because it was close to their radio transmitter from which they used to do propaganda, and therefore potentially was a major headquarters for the KLA at that particular time in their offensive in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give any boundaries that you were aware of for this area of command out of Malisevo, the villages essentially that were under the control of that headquarters. Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I know -- I suspected their control went north to the main Lapusnik-Pec-Pristina road, but I think it was a -- more a controlling headquarters or an attempt at a controlling headquarters to link the Drenica, Jablanica, and the western area together with this area of Malisevo and then going south to a village called Sedlare which was another headquarters down to Crnoljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So could you just indicate on the map for us the boundaries of that command area as you understood them at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I suspect, as I said, it went up to Lapusnik on this main road between Pristina and Pec and then also communicated with the village of Sedlare and Crnoljevo as well as moving back to Vojcnak up in the Drenica to Klina and then back on the corridor that I've talked about into back to Junik and over the border into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do you base those conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: On the fact that I visited all these other headquarters and on making a professional judgement as a soldier who's dealt with many counter-insurgency operations, that there needed to be some sort of command and control if the KLA was to be a composite and corporate tactical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you wish, it's actually a good time to finish if that's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now adjourn for this evening. If I could ask you to return tomorrow to continue your evidence. We resume at 9.00 in the morning. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
